By
The New Yorker
,
Shauna Lyon
, and
Rachel Syme
View the full
New Yorker Festival
event lineup and buy tickets.
The New Yorker Festival began in 2000, in celebration of the seventy-fifth anniversary of the magazine. It started a tradition of our writers and editors coming together with notable figures of the day, to bring alive what the magazine does in its pages—illuminate intricate ideas, complex histories, the latest news, and larger-than-life personalities—on stages across the city.
The New Yorker
turned a hundred last year, and the Festival, now in its twenty-seventh year, remains a multifaceted and sophisticated lens on what’s happening in culture, politics, and the literary world. Here is the schedule of the New Yorker Festival weekend. We hope you can join us.
Jump to:
Friday, October 23
|
Saturday, October 24
|
Sunday, October 25
Friday, October 23
Hannah Einbinder Talks with Rachel Syme
6 P.M., Webster Hall, at 125 E. 11th St.
The comedian and actress Hannah Einbinder is perhaps best known for her role as Ava Daniels, a forlorn yet subversive comedy writer, on HBO Max’s “Hacks,” for which she was nominated for five Emmys and four Golden Globes, winning one Emmy and a Critics Choice Award (and proving herself, beyond all doubt, not a hack). Einbinder’s début standup special, “Everything Must Go,” was released in 2024. This year, she starred in the gory, genre-bending film “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” which premièred at the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Queer Palm. Einbinder and the staff writer Rachel Syme sit down for what’s sure to be a lively chat.
The Art of Humor Writing
6 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre, at 150 W. 17th St.
A serious talk about a not-so-serious subject: Just what exactly turns a Whispers & Mumbles into a Shouts & Murmurs? Find out at this master class. The veteran Shouts & Murmurs writers Ian and Cora Frazier—who also happen to be father and daughter—join the articles editor Susan Morrison for a discussion about humor writing at a magazine that was founded, in 1925, as a “comic weekly.” Ian Frazier is a two-time recipient of the Thurber Prize for American Humor, for his essay collections “Coyote v. Acme” and “Lamentations of the Father.” Cora Frazier has contributed humor writing to The New Yorker since 2012. There will be readings, an audience Q. & A., and surely lots of shouts, murmurs, and, of course, laughter.
Ken Burns Talks with Michael Luo
6:30 P.M., the Joyce Theater, 175 8th Ave.
The filmmaker Ken Burns once said that “the great arrogance of the present is to forget the intelligence of the past.” In the course of forty-five years in the business, with investigations ranging from “The Civil War” and “The Vietnam War” to “Baseball” and “Country Music,” the documentarian has done his best to stay humble. Recently, he turned to the phenomenon that determined the course of our country—“The American Revolution.” Burns stops by the Festival to discuss his work with Michael Luo, an executive editor at the magazine, and the importance of chronicling history at a time when more and more is being written over and erased.
King Princess Talks with Amanda Petrusich and Performs
8:30 P.M., Webster Hall
“Girl Violence,” the third and most recent album by the singer and multi-instrumentalist Mikaela Straus, a.k.a. King Princess, ushered in a new era for her experiments in sonically fluid sapphic pop. If “1950,” her breakout single, from 2018, was emblematic of a vintage musical matrix that she has spent much of her career so far riffing on, “Girl Violence” longs to synthesize those sounds into something more peerless and forward-thinking. Straus, equal parts pop agitator and quirked-up rock star, wants to add more ferocity to songs of the queer canon, and she brings her learn-as-you-go energy to a performance and talk with the staff writer Amanda Petrusich.
Parker Posey Talks with Michael Schulman
8:30 p.m., the Joyce Theater
From party girl to teacher’s pet, Parker Posey, named Time’s “Queen of the Indies” in 1997, has delighted audiences for three decades with her exasperated-quirky-girl zingers and her uncanny embodiment of indignance. Last year, in Mike White’s third season of “The White Lotus,” Posey sunk her teeth into the plummy accent and soul-subsuming wealth of a Southern princess turned ill-equipped matriarch. This fall, she appears in Martin McDonagh’s new movie, “Wild Horse Nine,” as the wife of a C.I.A. agent who’s been dispatched to Easter Island, played by Sam Rockwell. At the Festival, Posey joins the staff writer Michael Schulman to talk about her career as a sui-generis actress.
Critics at Large Live, Featuring Vinson Cunningham, Naomi Fry, and Alexandra Schwartz
8:30 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
Are you in need of some guidance? Do you feel lost, culturally, socially, or just generally? Never fear: your favorite trio of culture gurus are here to help. The Critics at Large podcast hosts come to you live with their special segment “I Need a Critic!,” dishing out advice that they may or may not be qualified to give. Chime in with your questions, concerns, gripes, and hopes, and be prepared to have your life changed for the better—or, at the very least, to laugh a lot.
Saturday, October 24
Ann Patchett and Louise Erdrich Talk with Deborah Treisman
10 A.M., Webster Hall
Ann Patchett, the author of “Bel Canto” and, most recently, the Times best-seller “Whistler,” is the great conjurer of chosen families, crafting unlikely bonds between characters under duress. Louise Erdrich, a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians and the award-winning author of “The Night Watchman” and a new collection of stories, “Python’s Kiss,” is the premier voice memorializing the severed ties of family and culture among Native peoples. Both authors have invested in their home communities as owners of a local bookstore: Erdrich’s Birchbark Books, in Minneapolis, and Patchett’s Parnassus Books, in Nashville. The
New Yorker
fiction editor Deborah Treisman hosts the discussion.
The Future of A.I., Featuring Jill Lepore, Gideon Lewis-Kraus, and Andrew Marantz, with Joshua Rothman
10 A.M., the Joyce Theater
In early September, a former Anthropic employee said that the people building A.I. believe it could kill us all in less than ten years—a deeply unsettling proposition, especially for something that has already infiltrated our daily lives, in both obvious and invisible ways. Is that really where we’re headed? Is there any hope for regulation? And, if so, what will happen to all those chatbot boyfriends? The writers Jill Lepore, Gideon Lewis-Kraus, Andrew Marantz, and Joshua Rothman will parse through questions such as these, contemplating what the future holds for a technology that, for better or worse, seems here to stay.
Michael Douglas Talks with Ariel Levy
12:30 P.M., Webster Hall
Gordon Gekko embodied the nineteen-eighties Zeitgeist when he said—as delivered by a slick, suspender-clad Michael Douglas, in perhaps his most iconic role, in “Wall Street”—“Greed, for lack of a better word, is good.” Is it greedy to sustain a half-century career in Hollywood, win two Academy Awards, and receive A.F.I.’s Life Achievement Award? Maybe so, but then again Douglas also gives back, as a U.N. Messenger of Peace. You can read about it in his new memoir, “One Helluva Ride.” He speaks with the
New Yorker
staff writer Ariel Levy, who knows her way around an iconic octogenarian actor: she is Dustin Hoffman’s co-author for his forthcoming memoir, “Look at Me.”
Who Gets to Be an American?, Featuring Isabel Wilkerson, Jonathan Blitzer, and Jelani Cobb, with Michael Luo
12:30 P.M., the Joyce Theater
With an increase in ICE raids and violent arrests across the U.S., the topic of American identity is at the forefront of our political climate. What does it mean to be a part of this country, and how has that definition changed in recent years? Isabel Wilkerson, the author of “The Warmth of Other Suns” and “Caste,” joins the New Yorker writers Jonathan Blitzer and Jelani Cobb and executive editor Michael Luo for a roundtable discussion about the question of citizenship and the ways the Trump Administration has put its finger on the scale in the never-ending debate of belonging.
The Political Scene Live, Featuring David Plouffe, Susan B. Glasser, Jane Mayer, and Evan Osnos
3 P.M., Webster Hall
As the midterm elections approach, America’s future is up in the air and the stakes have never felt higher. Will the Democrats get themselves together and win the majority? If they do, will it make a tangible difference? Or will Republicans hold steady, insuring that President Trump stays bolstered by Congress? The country turned two hundred and fifty this year—will it last another quarter millennium? The hosts of The Political Scene podcast, Susan B. Glasser, Evan Osnos, and Jane Mayer, will be joined by the Democratic campaign strategist David Plouffe for a live taping, to discuss this pivotal moment in our history and how they think events might unfold.
Lorna Simpson Talks with Thelma Golden
3 P.M., the Joyce Theater
Visual art has the profound ability to act as a gateway and a solace, as a meditation and a statement. Perhaps no one is more representative of this breadth than the multimedia artist and photographer Lorna Simpson. One of the first African American female artists to exhibit at the Venice Biennale, Simpson has made a career capturing the conversation around the relationship between identity and memory. At this year’s Festival, she will sit down with Thelma Golden, the chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, to discuss the power of the image and the fulfillment and responsibility that come with creating.
The Pursuit of Equality
3 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
The feminist activist Barbara Smith co-founded the Combahee River Collective, a pioneering group that called attention to intersecting forms of oppression facing Black women in America; she also co-founded Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press, in 1980, to amplify the voices of people of color in publishing. She will join the staff writer Jia Tolentino to discuss the history of the feminist movement, the legacy of Gloria Steinem, and the role of activism in the modern world.
Cole Escola Talks with Julian Lucas
5:30 P.M., Webster Hall
Cole Escola burst onto the theatre scene in 2024, with their insanely irreverent, wickedly funny Off Broadway show, “Oh, Mary!,” in which they played Mary Todd Lincoln, a lush and a scamp, who just wants to sing cabaret. But Escola had been making uncanny videos (see “Pee Pee Manor,” about an especially unlucky real-estate agent) and TV appearances—on “Search Party,” “At Home with Amy Sedaris,” “Difficult People”—for years. “Oh, Mary!” is now enjoying an extended run on Broadway, with a rotating cast of Marys; Escola joins the staff writer Julian Lucas to talk about their career as an ingenious comedic scallywag.
Cartoon Improv, Judged by Josh Gondelman and Alison Leiby, Hosted by Emily Flake
5:30 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
The cartoonists Ellie Black, Ellis Rosen, Will Kiley Santino, and Drew Dernavich battle it out to prove that the pen is mightier than the sword, at this year’s installment of live cartoon improv. The comedians Josh Gondelman and Alison Leiby will serve as judge and jury, and the purportedly impartial cartoonist Emily Flake m.c.s. If you’re questioning this group’s qualifications for such a smackdown: Black has been contributing to The New Yorker since 2019; Rosen’s graphic-novel series about an evil squirrel will be released next year; Santino’s first book of cartoons will be published in 2027; and Dernavich has had more than three hundred cartoons in the magazine. Over on the judicial branch, Gondelman is a four-time Emmy Award-winning writer, and Leiby has contributed to television shows including “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel.” Flake is the recipient of the 2026 Thurber Award for Cartoon Art, so don’t heckle her.
Matthew Broderick Talks with Naomi Fry
6 P.M., the Joyce Theater
Life moves pretty fast for Matthew Broderick, the Tony-winning, Emmy-nominated actor who, for some, will always evoke the clarion call “Bueller . . . Bueller . . . Bueller.” Fresh off back-to-back theatrical performances, in “Ulster American,” at the Irish Rep, and “Celebrity Autobiography,” on Broadway, and looking ahead to an upcoming film aptly titled “The Best Is Yet to Come” (in which he reunites with his “Ferris Bueller” co-star Alan Ruck), Broderick sits down with Naomi Fry, a co-host of
The New Yorker’s
Critics at Large podcast and a staff writer covering pop culture. Broderick used to hang out with Marty Reisman, at a table-tennis parlor uptown, and Fry had a cameo in “Marty Supreme,” the Josh Safdie film based on Reisman’s exploits—does that count as six degrees of separation?
The Pixies Talk with Amanda Petrusich and Perform
8 P.M., Webster Hall
In the four decades since the Pixies dropped their début album, so much pop music has been shaped in their image. A few punks from Boston became the architects of a tectonic alt-rock sound that swung purposefully between noise and quiet, and the band’s 1988 masterpiece, “Surfer Rosa,” became a testament to its artsy thrasher sensibility. The music bore an awe--inspiring, cathartic quality that the group carries with it into its work today, most recently on the subtly charged 2024 album “The Night the Zombies Came.” In addition to diving into its catalogue for a live performance, the Pixies’ current foursome—Black Francis, Joey Santiago, David Lovering, and Emma Richardson—sits down with the staff writer Amanda Petrusich.
Benito Skinner Talks with Michael Schulman
8 P.M., the Joyce Theater
The comedian Benito Skinner—known as Benny Drama to his millions of followers on TikTok and Instagram—brings the drama to his conversation with the staff writer Michael Schulman. Skinner’s comedic stylings and vast collection of wigs are showcased in his original sketches and celebrity impressions; you might recognize the character “Jenni the TMI hairstylist,” along with nearly every Kardashian sister, from his videos. Skinner is the creator of the series “Overcompensating,” in which he stars as a fictionalized version of himself, closeted in college. In 2025, Skinner received the Critics Choice L.G.B.T.Q.+ Rising Star Award. All signs point to Skinner getting interviewed as, well, Benito Skinner, but an appearance by “Kris Jenner” is not out of the question.
Theater of War Productions Live, with Paul Dano and Bryan Doerries
8 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
Paul Dano has played a remarkable range of characters, from Brian Wilson, in the bio-pic “Love & Mercy,” to twin brothers in “There Will Be Blood.” For his next performance, he’ll read a
New Yorker
piece by Andrew Lipstein, about what it feels like to live with obsessive-compulsive disorder and its unruly symptoms. It’s a live production with Theater of War, a company that works with actors to present seminal texts. Its artistic director, Bryan Doerries, a writer and translator, will guide an audience discussion after the reading.
Trivia Night with The New Yorker, Hosted by Mina Kimes
8 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
Get ready for a night of quizzical fun for folks who read—or, at least, attempt to read (it counts)—the magazine cover to cover. The “Celebrity Jeopardy!” champion Mina Kimes hosts a rollicking evening of trivia crafted by members of
The New Yorker’s
Puzzles & Games department. Kimes won the top prize on “Celebrity Jeopardy! All-Stars” this year. And, when she’s not winning big, she’s an analyst on ESPN’s flagship football program, “NFL Live.” Pro tip: a sports-trivia category seems very likely.
Sunday, October 25
Min Jin Lee and Elizabeth Strout Talk with Katy Waldman
10 A.M., Webster Hall
Min Jin Lee dazzled the literary world with her second novel, “Pachinko,” chronicling the struggles of a Korean family in Japan during the turbulent twentieth century. Elizabeth Strout, the bard of Maine, is best known for detailing the complexities of small-town life in such books as “Olive Kitteridge” and “My Name Is Lucy Barton.” The writers’ stories, set in vastly different places, converge around the unique responsibilities shouldered by women. Lee’s much anticipated third novel, “American Hagwon,” released last month, charts a Korean family’s diaspora; Strout’s new novel, “The Things We Never Say,” follows the fallout of a boating accident in New England. They’ll chat with the
New Yorker
books writer Katy Waldman.
Portraits in Power, Featuring Isaac Chotiner, Clare Malone, Jane Mayer, and Lawrence Wright, with Daniel Zalewski
10 A.M., the Joyce Theater
Writing about any subject can be a delicate and formidable practice. When that subject happens to be one of the most powerful individuals or institutions in the world, it becomes a whole other challenge. In this Festival roundtable, the journalists Isaac Chotiner, Jane Mayer, Clare Malone, and Lawrence Wright will join Daniel Zalewski, an executive editor, to discuss what it’s like to excavate the hidden realities of titanic figures—whether it’s an architect of war (Chotiner), dark-money billionaires or Pete Hegseth (Mayer), Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. (Malone), or the Church of Scientology (Wright)—unearthing hidden details that the subjects would probably rather be left buried.
Ben Lerner and Valeria Luiselli Talk with Cressida Leyshon
12 P.M., the Joyce Theater
The MacArthur Fellows Ben Lerner and Valeria Luiselli share a proclivity for pushing the boundaries of fiction. Lerner, in his most recent novel, “Transcription,” tells his story via an interview unravelling in real time, the protagonist’s recording device breaking just before a crucial moment. Luiselli derives inspiration from sonic essays that she makes—capturing volcanic noise or the speech of strangers—and notes sound as a major inspiration for her latest book, “Beginning Middle End.” It’s up to the audience, and Cressida Leyshon,
The
New Yorker’s
deputy fiction editor, to distinguish between interview and autofiction when these two critically acclaimed authors sit down for a discussion.
Aaron Sorkin Talks with Tyler Foggatt
12:30 P.M., Webster Hall
The subject of influence has never been more relevant, or more complex. Enter Aaron Sorkin, with such projects under his belt as the TV show “The West Wing,” the movie “Steve Jobs,” and the play and subsequent film “A Few Good Men,” which is getting a Broadway revival this fall. Sorkin has made his career exposing the nuances of political, and personal, power dynamics. This year, he takes to the Festival stage, in a discussion with the senior editor Tyler Foggatt, just in time for his new film, “The Social Reckoning,” the follow-up to “The Social Network.” The movie is based on the true story of a whistle-blower who exposed Facebook’s secrets. There might just be a special guest appearance—though probably not from Mark Zuckerberg.
Ethan Hawke Talks with Emily Nussbaum
3 P.M., Webster Hall
Gen X underdog heartthrob, graphic novelist, Shakespearean actor, foil to Julie Delpy, and muse to Richard Linklater—Ethan Hawke wears many hats. Whether coming of age in “Dead Poets Society,” fighting to stay on the straight and narrow in “Training Day,” or aging before our eyes in “Boyhood,” Hawke is an inveterate entertainer. In last year’s “Blue Moon,” his ninth movie with Linklater, which earned him his fifth Academy Award nomination, he plays the lyricist Lorenz Hart, embodying a bitter and jealous endurer of humiliations, in a performance that Richard Brody called “exalted and startling.” He now stars in the TV crime drama “The Lowdown,” and a new film, “The Weight,” co-starring Russell Crowe, about a Depression-era road gang. He speaks with Emily Nussbaum, the magazine’s theatre critic.
Tessa Hadley and Colm Tóibín Talk with Deborah Treisman
3 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
Tessa Hadley and Colm Tóibín were born within a year of each other, with just the Irish Sea between them. Their writing, though both full of empathy and mounting tension, couldn’t be more distinct. Hadley, whose novella, “The Party,” will be published in paperback in 2027, pressurizes complicated domestic lives to the point where the sitting room is a war zone. Toíbín places his characters on cultural and institutional fault lines ripe for fictionalization, as in his next novel, “The Bridge,” publishing in December. In what promises to be a transatlantic treat, the
New Yorker
fiction editor Deborah Treisman talks with the pair.
Colson Whitehead Talks with Julian Lucas
3:30 P.M., the Joyce Theater
Colson Whitehead, a native New Yorker, won back-to-back Pulitzer Prizes for “The Underground Railroad” and “The Nickel Boys.” His most recent novels, which together constitute his Harlem Trilogy, are “Harlem Shuffle,” “Crook Manifesto,” and “Cool Machine.” This summer, the
New Yorker
staff writer Julian Lucas wrote an eight-thousand-word Profile of Whitehead, following him from a Manhattan bench with his name on it to his East Hampton home and a reading in Wyoming, ultimately shining light on the man that
Time
magazine called “America’s Storyteller.” Apparently, they only scratched the surface, so Lucas is returning for a deeper conversation with the award-winning writer.
Conan O’Brien Talks with David Remnick
5:30 P.M., Webster Hall
The flame-haired former late-night host Conan O’Brien swaps sides of the proverbial desk (there will be no desk) with the editor of
The New Yorker
, David Remnick. O’Brien, who is apparently a hundred-per-cent Irish, is much less than a hundred-per-cent lucky: he has been nominated for an Emmy Award thirty-six times, and won six. His most recent win was for his work as the host and executive producer of “Conan O’Brien Must Go,” on HBO Max, where he capped off one of the longest tenures in late-night-talk-show history, with a total of twenty-eight years as a host; he was the 2025 recipient of the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor. In addition to producing a podcast series, “Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend,” he has kindly agreed to host the Academy Awards once again, next year.
Dr. Becky and Emily Oster Talk with Dhruv Khullar
5:30 P.M., the Joyce Theater
The best-selling author Emily Oster will join Becky Kennedy—also known as Dr. Becky, the clinical psychologist who founded the parenting platform Good Inside—to talk with the physician and
New Yorker
contributing writer Dhruv Khullar about family matters. Oster’s data-driven books include “Expecting Better” and “Cribsheet,” works that have helped many an overwhelmed parent find the facts. Kennedy’s compassionate approach has proved similarly useful for caregivers trying to raise resilient, confident kids. If you have children, you won’t want to miss this panel.
Mahershala Ali Talks with Vinson Cunningham
5:30 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
From “Moonlight” to “Green Book,” “House of Cards” to “True Detective,” Mahershala Ali doesn’t just steal scenes—he runs away with the project and leaves the indelible mark of his character onscreen. Among many accolades, he is the first Muslim man to win an Academy Award. Before conquering Hollywood, Ali played Division I basketball (standing at six feet four) and released rap albums under the name Prince Ali. This fall, Ali stars in Bassam Tariq’s thriller, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” He will be in conversation with Vinson Cunningham, a critic at the magazine and a fellow basketball obsessive.
Atsuko Okatsuka and Chris Fleming Talk with Emma Allen
8 P.M., Webster Hall
The standup comedians and general goofballs Atsuko Okatsuka and Chris Fleming join the cartoon editor Emma Allen for a lively discussion that may or may not end with Okatsuka’s viral Drop Challenge. Okatsuka and Fleming are known for their signature locks: Okatsuka for her coiffed bowl cut and Fleming for his cascading curls (tragically shorn for a recent role). Fleming, a self-proclaimed “showpig” who got his start on YouTube, playing a stay-at-home mom named Gayle, and who recently appeared in the first season of “Widow’s Bay,” released an Emmy-nominated standup special, “Chris Fleming: Live at the Palace,” this year. Okatsuka’s second special, “Father,” premièred last year, nabbing a Webby Award for best standup.
Mariska Hargitay Talks with Rachel Syme
8 P.M., the T. Rowe Price Theatre
Mariska Hargitay, coming off a successful turn hosting the Emmys, is the embodiment of a safe space for many people who know her as Captain Olivia Benson, the character that she’s played on “Law & Order: S.V.U.” for twenty-seven years. In real life, she founded the Joyful Heart Foundation, dedicated to changing society’s response to sexual assault and domestic violence. Beyond the realm of criminal justice, Hargitay recently put out the documentary “My Mom Jayne,” and made her Broadway début, in “Every Brilliant Thing.” She speaks with the
New Yorker
staff writer Rachel Syme, who writes about Hollywood and fashion, and who will hopefully address Hargitay’s record-breaking number of outfit changes at the Emmys.
Wynton Marsalis Talks with Nick Trautwein and Performs
8:30 P.M., the Joyce Theater
The distinguished New Orleans-born musician Wynton Marsalis has worn many hats: dynamic trumpeter, intrepid composer and bandleader, and artistic director for Jazz at Lincoln Center, which he founded, in 1987. He is a Pulitzer Prize winner and a multi-Grammy holder—the only to win in both jazz and classical in the same year—but, chiefly, he is an ambassador for those traditional forms across generations. His most recent recordings with the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, “We the People” and “Let Freedom Swing,” seek the intersection of arts appreciation and political involvement. Marsalis samples his expansive repertoire in performance and is joined in conversation by the senior editor Nick Trautwein.
In the Neighborhood
Shauna Lyon
on fun spots in Chelsea.
There has been a tremendous amount of recent development in Chelsea, but, ever the story in New York City, as beloved old places close their doors, new favorites emerge. A wonderland of park space has been created along the Hudson River, where you can partake in kayaking or jogging or sunbathing, or escape to leaf-peep the maples and dogwoods of
Little Island
. You could spend hours taking in art of all kinds in the still thriving
gallery district
in the far West Twenties; for your book fix, stop in at
Printed Matter, Inc.
(231 Eleventh Ave.), heavily stocked with zines and art journals, or at the well-curated, charmingly tiny
192 Books,
on Tenth Avenue at Twenty-first Street. Over on Seventh Avenue,
Books N’ Cup
is a cozy new coffee shop; if the literary environs cause a sudden urge to type the old-fashioned way, you might check
Gramercy Typewriter Co.,
on Seventeenth Street, for vintage models for sale. Food meccas include
Pier 57
(hit Nom Wah for legendary dim sum, or LoLo’s on the Water for the fish fry) and, of course,
Chelsea Market
(try Miznon’s pita cheeseburger and roasted cauliflower, and Ayada’s mango sticky rice). For drinks and elevated snacks close to the Joyce,
Konban
is an adventurous Japanese izakaya; the
Lobby Bar
in the storied Hotel Chelsea serves a mean margarita, and
Shukette
throws a party complete with addictive dips and wood-fired breads. A jaunt in Chelsea would not be complete without a stroll on the
High Line
, pausing near Thirtieth Street to contemplate a twenty-seven-foot Buddha sculpture, by Tuan Andrew Nguyen. Keep walking north for a treat at
Mercado Little Spain,
in Hudson Yards, where you can sample the platonic ideal of
pan con tomate
, on the correct Catalan
pan de cristal
, and José Andrés’s famous bursting Liquid Olives, a throwback to the heyday of molecular gastronomy—remember that?
Rachel Syme
on East Village treasures.
The East Village is, let’s be honest, not what it once was, but then, is anywhere in New York? The city is the rare global metropolis that has little preciousness about living in the past; the only constant is change. The East Village is no longer the city’s preëminent gritty haven for punks, artists, and eccentrics—St. Mark’s Place, once a hashish-scented playground full of leather clubs and piercing studios, is now a manicured promenade where young professionals go to drink spritzes en plein air—but that doesn’t mean it’s without delights, both old and new. If you’re in the area for The New Yorker Festival, you could do far worse than to dip into some still-going classic establishments, such as Veselka, for borscht and pierogi;
John’s of 12th Street,
for penne alla vodka; or
Veniero’s,
for coffee and cannoli. If you’re after even more sugar, you can stop into
Lady Wong Patisserie
for delicate little cakes,
Librae Bakery
for Middle Eastern pastries, or
SLIK
for Scandinavian pick-and-mix candy. Need a drink?
Rabbit Books & Bar
is a new spot that is half bookstore and half low-lit lounge, or there’s
Madeline’s Martini,
a veritable temple to the classic cocktail. The East Village is also a vintage shopper’s haven: there’s
Tokio7
for designer clothes,
Fabulous Fanny’s
for glasses, and
Cure Thrift
for delightful bric-a-brac. (Hot tip: Cure is where the iconic downtown magpie Amy Sedaris drops off her gently used goods.) After a brisk stroll through
Tompkins Square Park,
you can hop across the street to the cult-favorite
Superiority Burger
—everything on the menu is vegetarian, but you won’t miss the meat. Lastly, try ducking into
Casey Rubber Stamps,
founded in 1979, in the West Village, and a neighborhood fixture since 2003. Some of the old Village is still lurking there, if you squint.

Facing the Death Penalty
The cases of Christa Pike and Nidal Hasan show how vanishingly fine the line is between a routine execution and an unbearable one.
By
Amy Davidson Sorkin
Photo illustration by Cristiana Couceiro; Source photographs from Bloomberg / Getty; Picture Alliance / Getty
In recent weeks, tolerance for the death penalty, as it is carried out in the United States, has been sorely tested twice. On September 30th, the state of Tennessee bungled its attempt to kill Christa Pike, who survived two injections of pentobarbital. Eight days later, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gleefully invited the nation to tune in, via live stream, for the death by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, scheduled for December 3rd. It took another week for President Donald Trump to call off the broadcast, amid an uproar. He said, in a Truth Social post, that, though he thought a live stream would send a useful message about America’s strength, he accepted that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch.” He made it sound like a programming preference, not a moral one.
Pike’s botched execution did not result in Tennessee looking strong. Though the event was not public, there were watch-rooms connected to the death chamber. In one sat May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer, who was nineteen years old when, in 1995, Pike, then eighteen, beat and killed her, with the help of two teen-age accomplices. A group of journalists, designated as “media witnesses,” sat in another. At 7:26
P.M
., according to the journalists, a black curtain fitted to a large glass window was pulled back, and they saw Pike strapped to a gurney. Prison personnel had already set I.V. lines and left the chamber to begin the flow of pentobarbital from yet another room.
Through a microphone, the journalists listened as Pike spoke what were meant to be her last words—about love—and sang with her Buddhist spiritual adviser. Then they heard her ask if her arm was supposed to hurt as much as it did—as if her veins would burst. She raised her head and kicked her legs, knocking a sheet off the gurney. At 7:46
P.M.
, the curtain was closed. It was opened three minutes later, presumably so that the witnesses could see the effects of a second, backup dose. What they saw was a woman who was clearly alive. At 8:05
P.M
., the curtain closed again, but the microphone stayed on, leaving the journalists with the sound of Pike’s labored breathing and snoring. When, at 8:53
P.M.
, they were finally told to go, they were pretty sure that Pike was not dead.
“I cannot emphasize enough how much of whatever just happened happened behind a closed curtain,” Steven Hale, of the Nashville
Banner
, said at a press conference afterward. In the days that followed, more details came out. Before the curtain opened, according to Pike’s lawyers, medical workers had struggled with the I.V., using at least seven needles. A working theory is that a line was misplaced, or that a vein was blown, causing the pentobarbital to spread into the surrounding tissue. Pike’s lawyers had warned, in court filings, that she had blood and circulatory conditions that put her at risk for precisely this outcome. (They have also argued that sexual violence Pike endured as a child should have weighed more heavily in her sentencing.)
Lethal injection is the most common method of capital punishment in the U.S. And yet, according to the Associated Press, I.V. problems have derailed more than half a dozen executions since 2009, including one in Tennessee this past May. Pike’s case stands out because the execution team proceeded with the injection of pentobarbital anyway. The level of recklessness in that decision will no doubt be a focus of the investigation that Bill Lee, the governor of Tennessee, has ordered. Lee has delayed other pending executions, but he has not yet said if the state will try again to kill Pike, who was unconscious for several days before waking up in a hospital, confused and in pain. It’s unclear if she will fully recover. Last week, it emerged that even the call from the prison for an ambulance was mishandled. Pike’s lawyers have described what happened to her as torture. An unanswerable question is how the night might have ended had no one been watching.
There is a distinction, of course, between insisting on witnesses and staging a spectacle. Hegseth promoted the live stream in an interview with Jack Posobiec, a right-wing influencer, on the deck of the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln. Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist, shot and killed twelve fellow-soldiers (one of whom was pregnant) and a civilian at Fort Hood, in 2009, ahead of a deployment to Afghanistan. “No-brainer. Execution by firing squad,” Hegseth said. “And we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” There hasn’t been a public execution in the United States in almost ninety years. Hasan is confined to a wheelchair; he was paralyzed as a result of the firefight that ended his shooting spree. He has said that he wants to be a martyr, and one of the many problems with Hegseth’s plan was that it might have helped him get his wish. But the more profound issue was the grubby death-cult revelry that a live stream would entail.
Even some supporters of capital punishment, including a number of Republican lawmakers, seemed repelled by the prospect. In recent years, only a few countries have been known to conduct public executions, notably Iran and Afghanistan. Meanwhile, of the thirty-eight nations in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, only two—the U.S. and Japan—regularly carry out death sentences at all. (China, which is not in the O.E.C.D., does, too.)
The Eighth Amendment forbids “cruel and unusual punishments”; the Supreme Court has long said that the death penalty is permissible, even as it has gradually tightened its standard. In 1988, for example, the Court banned the death penalty for crimes committed by someone under the age of sixteen. The Justices only raised the age to eighteen in 2005. But such adjustments, welcome as they are, cannot conceal the essential brutality of the enterprise; the Pike and Hasan cases show how vanishingly fine the line is between a routine execution and an unbearable one.
When Markwayne Mullin, the Secretary of Homeland Security, was asked about Hegseth’s live stream before Trump called it off, he said, “No one has to watch.” In the age of TikTok and autoplay videos, that’s simply not true. But Mullin’s reply also seemed to convey a hope that no one would notice the actions and the character of this Administration, with officials, such as Hegseth, who appear unashamed of their worst instincts. One can’t always look away. ♦

epub_7.title: Chapter 7
epub_7.text:
Room With a View
Your Next Vacay Is . . . the Strait of Hormuz?
The ad agency M+C Saatchi has been working to boost tourism in the war-torn region. One of its inspo pics is Anthony Bourdain in sunglasses.
By
Charles Bethea
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
In August, six months into the escalating war between the United States and Iran (and their various regional allies), the global advertising agency M+C Saatchi put out a press release. It had become the “creative agency partner” for the Ras al-Khaimah tourism authority, following “a highly competitive multi-stage pitch process.” Ras al-Khaimah is among the seven emirates that make up the United Arab Emirates. Its northern coasts, known for their golden-white-sand beaches and mangrove forests, abut the Strait of Hormuz. At least two dozen vessels, many of them commercial tankers carrying crude oil and gas, have been attacked this month as they’ve tried to pass through the strait. But, war or no war, M+C Saatchi would endeavor to lure tourists here.
The press release noted that the Ras al-Khaimah tourism authority was “one of the region’s most ambitious,” but it did not mention the ongoing conflict centered on the nearby strait. Instead—beneath a photograph of smiling young people sitting on sumptuous rugs and drinking colorful beverages on the edge of a cliff overlooking a strait-like body of water—text announced that M+C Saatchi would be launching “a new destination proposition” for the area over the following three years. The agency had been chosen, it explained, for its “belief in Cultural Power” and its ability to bring together “specialists . . . to deliver connected thinking across every touchpoint.”
A separate M+C Saatchi document—this one internal—was a request for proposals, inviting content creators to come up with “a destination campaign that changes how people think” about the war zone, through “a fresh approach to destination storytelling.” It envisioned a campaign with an “observational, journalistic approach” that “feels more like a beautifully crafted documentary than a tourism commercial.” What kind of documentary, exactly? “Think Anthony Bourdain’s curiosity,” the brief went on, under a photo of Bourdain in sunglasses, leaning out of a train window, alongside stock images of starry skies, ocean swimmers, and a mountain climber on a sweeping ridge. “Space. Discovery. Contrast,” the document continued vaguely. Desired tone? “The emotional honesty of a travel journal.” Project bidders were advised to “be comfortable following something unexpected if it reveals a better truth.” The instructions concluded, “Show us moments that couldn’t happen anywhere else.”
One photographer who saw the internal M+C Saatchi document suspected that it had been created by artificial intelligence. “The Bourdain bit was a dead giveaway for A.I.,” he said. “Like, come on.” He went on, “If they want someone to come up with the creative direction and shoot the campaign—in a war zone—they’re gonna need to find a content creator with a solid ring light and a working air-defense system.” He added, “Feels fraught.” President Donald Trump recently told the United Nations that he was considering whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” and “drive them into hell,” which, one presumes, would not bode well for photographers or tourists in the region.
Another photographer who reviewed M+C Saatchi’s document said, “If the request is to work in an active war zone, you’d like to think they’d be up front about it. I had to do a Google search to confirm.” A travel-industry veteran who saw the R.F.P. said, “Not only are you possibly getting bombed, but you’re basically sending hundreds or thousands of other people—tourists—into it. Wild times.”
According to a recent article in
Arabian Business
, a Middle Eastern news outlet that covers real estate, there are “lots of rooms available” in hotels “overlooking the Strait of Hormuz.” A room at the four-star Azimut Hotel Musandam, just across the border, in Oman, was recently going for seventy-two dollars a night. An online writeup of the hotel said, “Ride an Omani Dhow cruising the sea coast in the Strait of Hormuz.” The construction of the Wynn al-Marjan Island, a multibillion-dollar gaming resort on a man-made island sixty miles southwest of the strait, has also slowed. “This picture could shift,” a Wynn executive told investors earlier this year, during a dour earnings call.
Still, tourism around the strait has not completely ground to a halt. A recent review of the budget-tier Ras al-Khaimah Hotel described it as a “perfect staycation,” despite the fact that “the swimming pool is average.” ♦

epub_8.title: Chapter 8
epub_8.text:
The Boards
Bill Irwin Is the O.G. Clown
Fresh from playing the Cyclops in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” the rubber-limbed actor chats about reviving and starring in Molière’s “The Imaginary Invalid” on Broadway.
By
Henry Alford
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
Seldom does the theatre adequately address the topic of enemas. But Molière’s “The Imaginary Invalid,” which Bill Irwin has adapted and is starring in on Broadway, will serve all your peristaltic needs: Irwin’s hypochondriacal title character encounters a syringe the size of a submachine gun. “Molière pushes the envelope,” Irwin said the other day, on a park bench in Union Square, where he and his wife, Martha, and their Ridgeback mix, Zelda, had just dropped off their compost. “I worry that we might have too many enema references, though.”
Irwin typically skews self-deprecatory in conversation. He first came on most people’s radars through his baggy-pants clowning on Broadway and, later, on “Sesame Street,” as Mr. Noodle, radiating a kind of doomed naïveté. “In clowning, there’s a paradigm,” he said. “Chaplin and Keaton and Harold Lloyd—the young guy who’s going to make it in life, or who’s going to impress his mother or girlfriend.” He went on, “But you get a little older, and you realize, I don’t do that anymore. I’m no use to that genre anymore.” Irwin, who is seventy-six, had on sneakers and a loose blue jacket. As his recent roles suggest, he is better served performing the catalyst or the antagonist. In “The Imaginary Invalid,” his character is trying to marry his daughter off to a doctor against her will. In this summer’s “The Odyssey,” as the Cyclops, he prays to his father, Poseidon, to curse Odysseus and his men after they’ve broken into his cave, blinded him, and, as Irwin put it, “fucked with my cheese.”
When Irwin first met with the film’s director, Christopher Nolan, to discuss playing the Cyclops, he asked if he’d be wearing a mask. “Chris said, ‘Probably.’ He didn’t know yet. He often doesn’t know.” In Nolan’s 2014 film, “Interstellar,” Irwin voiced and did much of the puppetry behind
TARS
, the robot that resembles an enormous metallic KitKat bar. For “The Odyssey,” Irwin, wearing full-body makeup and prosthetics, shot with a thirty-six-foot-tall puppet in a cave in Greece and in a miniature mockup of the cave in Culver City. “Tom Holland said Chris was the most meticulously prepared shoot-from-the-hip director he’d ever worked with,” he recalled.
Irwin initially told Nolan that he might be too old to play the Cyclops. (“You need a guy who doesn’t need kneepads.”) He had no such anxieties with “The Imaginary Invalid”: Molière, who played the title role himself in 1673, wrote the play while he was in a tubercular decline, creating a part in which he could cough a lot while staying in character. Irwin was not rattled by the fact that Molière died after his fourth performance. Asked how his own health is, Irwin replied, “It is a daily question. But good, I think.” He added, “Martha and I ride Citi Bikes, and I’m a more law-abiding cyclist than I normally would be.”
He was pleased to hear, from his “Imaginary Invalid” co-star Rachel Bloom, the co-creator and star of TV’s “Crazy Ex-Girlfriend,” that clowning is huge in L.A. these days. “She said that the same young guys who, eighteen months ago, would have used a different label—‘improv’ or something—are now all ‘I’m hard-core clown,’ ” he noted. His years in the trenches have fostered compassion: “I have great sympathy for anyone who has signed on to be Ronald McDonald. He’s the least tuned-in-to-clown-history example of clowning. I learned at the Ringling school that the lower lip is the expressive lip. Like, tonight, when I do the show, I’ll go”—he twisted his lower lip—“because that’s the one that defines the expression. Ronald McDonald’s makeup is all upper lip, and that’s why he’s kind of frozen-looking.”
He talked about losing himself in a role. “When I watch myself, there’s usually more of me than I’d like there to be,” he said. Many of his roles feature an element of absence—from his early work as a silent clown to the strangled emotion he brought to assorted Beckett projects to his Tony-winning turn as George in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” What he holds back is what defines him. When a passerby in the park—a former colleague—called out, “Bill! I saw you!,” Irwin replied, “Hey, man! Did you come? You dog, you.”
Confused, the man asked, “What do you mean?”
“Oh, I’m doing a show.”
“No, I mean, I saw you just now. I haven’t seen you in decades.”
“Well, shit on a stick.” ♦

epub_9.title: Chapter 9
epub_9.text:
The Pictures
Josh Safdie’s Top Ten (or So) N.Y.C. Films
The director stops by the Two Palms studio to sign prints of a list of his favorite New York movies—“Taxi Driver,” “Do the Right Thing,” and some you wouldn’t expect.
By
Bruce Handy
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
Josh Safdie directed and co-wrote “Marty Supreme.” He also co-directed (with his younger brother, Benny) and co-wrote “Uncut Gems.” Like the heroes of those films, Safdie is a native New Yorker and a very fast, very entertaining talker. He demonstrated this one recent morning, when he arrived at Two Palms, a sprawling printmaking studio in SoHo where he was set to sign, number, and date a run of silk-screen prints that he’d created in collaboration with the studio’s artisans. The prints, fifty in total (plus multiple artists’ and printers’ proofs), were laid out in tranches of six on carefully prepared worktables. Four Staedtler 2B pencils were ready to go—sharpened and then slightly dulled, to prevent puncturing the paper. (Safdie, who is particular about writing implements, had test-driven possible pencils earlier.) Small talk was dispensed with quickly, but then the director, forty-two years old with collar-length hair and a beard that stops just shy of scraggly—you could add him to the cover of Dylan and the Band’s “Basement Tapes” LP and no one would notice—began reminiscing about a nearby office he’d had years ago, in the same building as “Greta and Lena.” And bingo: he was off on a ping-ponging monologue.
He brought up Jonas Mekas, the underground filmmaker and co-founder of Anthology Film Archives—a “genius,” but also a “difficult” boss. (Safdie’s screenwriting partner once worked at Anthology as a projectionist.) Mekas led him to Fluxus, the nineteen-sixties arts movement in which Yoko Ono played a prominent part. Fluxus led to “a girl I used to live with” whose father had served as Fluxus’s organizer and later worked with Ono and John Lennon. The father had “this house that’s packed with crap. Not crap. Artifacts.” Among those artifacts was a Nudie suit given to Lennon by his pal Harry Nilsson. “I just had to try it on because I was super skinny then,” Safdie said. (Note: He’s still pretty slender.) “We did a little photo series,” he continued. “Wow. Anyway.”
Twenty minutes after he walked in the door, the signing began. Saloni Shah, a Two Palms employee who otherwise guides the studio’s work with experimental materials, called out Safdie’s progress—“Three of fifty . . . four of fifty . . .”—to keep him on track. The print, titled “Top 10 NYC Films,” had begun life as an eight-and-a-half-by-seven-and-a-half-inch notecard on which the director listed his favorite movies shot in New York, intended as a gift for friends. “I was never going to do just ten,” he admitted. But Safdie kept adding more films, and then still more, in block letters using pens of different colors. He underlined some titles, highlighted others, changed his mind, appended qualifications here and there. The document ended up looking like Grandma’s favorite recipe card, if Grandma had O.C.D. and a pen fetish.
“He was going on about ‘Alas, poor Yorick,’ and I didn’t want to say anything, but I was thinking, Dude, you don’t exactly seem to be thriving right now yourself . . .”
Cartoon by Jason Adam Katzenstein
David Lasry, Two Palms’ founder, contrasted the studio’s collaboration with Safdie to past work with artists like Chuck Close and Sol LeWitt: “They’re conceptual artists. They made rules for making art. Josh started with rules, but then he lost control of it because of his enthusiasm.” The task for the printmakers, led by Erik Hougen, Jeremy Ruiz, and Tom Smith, was to reproduce the jottings, corrections, and accidental smears on Safdie’s notecard as faithfully as possible, and also to scale it up in size. The process took two months and involved twenty silk-screen passes, plus collage, handstamps, and stencils for a special paint designed to crackle in imitation of Safdie’s blots of Wite-Out.
Films you’d expect made the cut (“Taxi Driver,” “Do the Right Thing,” “Dog Day Afternoon”), along with some you might not (“Cruising,” a pair of Troma Z movies). Only a week earlier, Safdie had decided to add the 1978 Richard Gere picture “Bloodbrothers,” even though the silk screening had already been completed. Neither Safdie nor Lasry was sure how many films were on the finished prints, or even which ones. “Do I have ‘Wild Style’ on here?” Safdie asked, referencing the seminal 1983 hip-hop movie. He did. He counted the films, tallying a hundred and fifteen—plus another twelve he had added with asterisks, because they were only partially filmed in New York (“The Godfather,” parts I and II) or were, one way or another, “in communication with” the city (the Hoboken-set “On the Waterfront”). Lasry dryly suggested a new title: “115 of the Top 10 NYC Films.”
The signing completed, Safdie sat with a cup of coffee and mentioned several movies he’d chosen not to include, one being “Manhattan,” a film that he admitted he “didn’t really love.” This wasn’t a knock on Woody Allen; Safdie had included “Broadway Danny Rose” and “Hannah and Her Sisters.” Allen, he said, is “one of the most New York filmmakers.” He paused. “Do I not have ‘Radio Days’ on my list? Oh, my God. I’m so embarrassed if it’s not on.” He got up to check. A moan: “I fucking don’t have ‘Radio Days’!” He consulted with Lasry, and within minutes the team had begun to create a rubber stamp so that “Radio Days” could be added to the finished (and, in some cases, already sold) prints, wedged in tiny and tight, right below “The Apartment.” ♦

epub_10.title: Chapter 10
epub_10.text:
Backstage Dept.
The Furry Prima Donna of “La Bohème”
Wanda the Donkey regularly steals the show at the Met’s most popular production. Here’s an inside look at her creative process.
By
Sarah Larson
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
On Amsterdam Avenue by the Metropolitan Opera House—a day before
Mayor Mamdani
announced his new free-opera-tickets initiative—two supernumerary performers in Puccini’s “La Bohème,” the Met’s most popular opera, disembarked from a horse trailer. Wanda, a donkey, and Max, a horse, split their time between a farm upstate and a stable in the Bronx. They’re “Bohème” veterans, and that morning was the season’s first full-dress rehearsal. “Here she is!” the animals’ agent, Nancy Novograd, a silver-haired former lawyer in sunglasses and a dark jacket, said. “There’s Wanda! Isn’t she a cutie? And Max is handsome and magnificent.” Wanda is gray, with white-grizzled accents, upturned ears, and a classically round torso; Max is a glossy bay, with a mane like Moe Howard’s bangs. “And the personalities are what count, right?” Novograd went on. “It’s always personality. For animals, we call it temperament.” She owns a company called All Tame Animals (“Anything from elephants to insects”), which matches productions with show-biz-ready beasts. “Bold is the key,” she said. “It’s the same with dogs. If they’re not confident, they can’t do it.” Wanda, eighteen, has a temperament of supreme unflappability. “A lot of donkeys won’t let you touch their feet,” Novograd said. “She’s special in that way.” Wanda’s other steady gig is an annual Palm Sunday procession at a church uptown.
In the parking garage, the animals were unfazed by noisy construction and enthusiastic fans. “
Hey
, the stars of the show!” a man said. A handler made a call: “Hi, we have the horse and donkey. Are you ready?” The stars proceeded through the “horse door,” up a ramp, and down a hallway with a red vinyl floor, passing costume racks and photos of “Das Rheingold” and “Turandot.” Onstage, they crossed a set strewn with paper snowflakes where, in Act III, Mimì and Rodolfo would sing “Addio, dolce svegliare” (“Farewell, sweet awakening”) and agree to break up in the spring. The group reached the cavernous stage-left space, where they spend Act I, and stood alongside two-story façades of Parisian apartment buildings and, for the evening’s updated production of Mozart’s “Così Fan Tutte,” Coney Island-style backdrops (hot-dog stand, bearded-lady sideshow). “I’m coming back tonight for ‘Così,’ ” Novograd said. “I’ve got a snake in it.”
Novograd has worked with the Met since 1998, when she was hired “to bring the horses and work with Mr. Zeffirelli, for ‘Carmen.’ ” Once, she recalled, he’d singled out a nervous equestrian: “You! You look like you’re going to your husband’s funeral on the back of another man’s horse!” Novograd laughed. “He was so attentive to detail.” Opera’s animal friendliness has waned a bit. “ ‘Aida’ should have elephants,” Novograd said. Gone are “Carmen” ’s and “Aida” ’s horses and “Hansel and Gretel” ’s cat. Then again, “Così Fan Tutte” usually lacks a snake; this one has a boa constrictor.
A soundproof curtain descended, and the opera began. Only occasionally did a note seep through. Wanda’s handler, a young woman in a Ford Mustang T-shirt, helped Wanda into a pointy red hat with ear holes, a neck ruffle, and a fancy blanket with a “P” on it—Zeffirelli originals—and sat on Mimì’s fainting couch. She ate a granola bar and checked her phone. Wanda, mildly curious, nuzzled the phone. Wanda plays the donkey of a toy seller, Parpignol (Gregory Warren); she pulls his lavishly painted cart outside Café Momus on Christmas Eve. Warren, a tenor, arrived in a pink harlequin outfit, with knee socks and buckled shoes. His stubble was obscured by a full face of clown makeup. “I’m also in ‘Lincoln in the Bardo,’ ” he said. He picked up a Napoleon-style hat with pink hair attached, put it on his head, and fastened the chin strap. “In this, my line is ‘
Ecco i giocattoli di Parpignol!
’—‘Here are Parpignol’s toys!’ ” he added.
The soundproof curtain came up, and a crew in T-shirts (Knicks, Amoeba Music) loaded out the garret set. The animals and handlers headed to the stage-left wing and waited alongside smartly dressed, whispering children; Warren did some stretching and bouncing. Onstage, two hundred townsfolk sang, and a stilt walker strolled. Then the big moment: Parpignol sang, Wanda pulled the toy cart onstage (guided by her handler, now in a cloak and top hat), and kids swarmed them, clamoring for treats. Wanda remained chill. Back offstage, she waited for Max to drop off Musetta as a pit crew swiftly removed her ruffle and her hat. Soon, with Max, she was back in the trailer, chomping on a peppermint. “Goodbye!” Novograd said. She’d return that night for the snake-handling. Meanwhile, “we have a dog with a late call today on ‘NCIS: New York.’ He’s a fabulous dog, a blue-pit mix, and he is beloved wherever he goes.” ♦
