Daunt might never have left the bank had it not been for Steward. She had fallen in love with a diplomat’s son, an adventurous student of history. The prospect of spending the rest of her life with a man who nattered on about yield curves filled her with despair. Daunt weighed his options. “I thought, If I’m going to take myself out of an office job, I have to do something for myself and tie it to my interests,” he said.
He liked to read, he reasoned, and he liked to travel. When he planned a trip, the first thing he did was to go to the bookstore and immerse himself in the area’s history and literature. Usually, that meant a search through both the history and fiction sections, each a jumble of books from everywhere and every age. “If you read ‘Suite Française,’ the Irène Némirovsky novel, well, then you want to read about the Occupation, you want to read about collaboration, and so on—but nobody put those books together,” he said. What if there were regional sections in which all these elements—novels, poetry, histories, guidebooks—were grouped? Daunt likes to describe this as the moment when he set his mind on the idea of a bookstore, though Bonneville recalls it differently. “My abiding memory at university is of him saying, ‘I’m going to get a job in the city for a couple of years, learn about business, and then open a bookshop,’ ” he told me. “I said, ‘Don’t be ridiculous.’ ”
In 1989, Daunt, back in London, toured the run-down site of a former antiquarian shop on Marylebone High Street—a long, double-height chamber with stained glass and skylights, a balcony-like mezzanine, and light pouring onto two stories of bookshelves. “There it was, dusty, full of crap,” he told me. “Bookstores are usually just shops that you convert, but this one was
purpose-built
for bookselling.” He opened his shop that winter. He was twenty-six and, as he put it to me, “quite interested in trying to make a different kind of bookstore work.”
One Sunday morning in August, I stopped by the original Daunt Books twenty minutes after opening. The store was already crowded. In the double-height room, the dark-wood shelves were labelled, in gold capitals, with the regions of the world (“
CZECH & SLOVAK REPS
,” “
POLAND
”). A middle-aged woman sat in a high-backed armchair and read a few dozen pages of Rachel Blackmore’s novel “
Costanza
.” On the mezzanine, young people alternately browsed and posed for Beatles-style photographs taken from below. At the “
ITALY
” shelves, a young American girl intoned to her father from an introductory Italian-language book: “
Io sono alta, ho i capelli castani e un po’ lunghi.
”
When Daunt Books opened, on the Ides of March, in 1990, it was an inauspicious moment to start an internationally themed bookstore. Less than a year earlier, two London shops had been bombed for selling Salman Rushdie’s “
Satanic Verses
.” But Daunt thought that reading was headed in a global direction, and, broadly, time proved him correct. Successful authors once boasted of the number of languages into which they were translated, but that is no longer seen to be a marker of ubiquity—not because English-language work isn’t read but because the Anglosphere has grown. By 2045, in some projections, a plurality of English readers will live in China.
None of that helped the store’s début. “It was a disaster,” Daunt recalled. That year, the United Kingdom tipped into recession, and Marylebone High Street became a retail wasteland. “It was a staff of three or four of us in this quite big shop,” Wolstencroft, who is now the manager of the Marylebone store, told me. He had been training to be a lawyer when Daunt enlisted him to help set up the place, and he never left. No one had experience in the trade, and most of the shop’s signature features emerged from trial and error and the uncertainty of the market.
At the start, they placed their titles cover out because they didn’t have enough stock to fill their shelves. They began arranging books on tables, in a set of stacks known as “the pyramid.” Circular tables were ideal, they found, because customers passed them in a rounding motion, keeping their attention on the surfaces for longer. Daunt deplored the dingy norm of London’s independent bookstores and spent months keying up his lighting. Then he niggled with the shelves. An incline of exactly three degrees, he discovered, put books in the optimal path of light. (At Waterstones, the angle was revised to 4.5 degrees.) To fill gaps and corners, he made display risers covered with a very British William Morris fabric involving leaves, flowers, and uneasy-looking birds. (“Those patterns are, like, lodged in the back of my brain,” the literary agent Juliet Mushens, who has spent a lot of time in Daunt’s shops, told me.) Wolstencroft and Daunt noticed that pedestrians tuned out cluttered shop windows, so they loaded theirs with a single title at a time, and decorated them thematically, like department stores’. In the early days, London was still a city of smokers, and Daunt would count cigarette butts on the sidewalk to gauge how many passersby had stopped to look.
What emerged was a model of bookselling both knowledgeable and precisely retail-focussed. Laura Macaulay, a bookseller in the two-thousands, recalled Daunt telling her, “Everything we do has to make a profit.” Staffers were encouraged to read prolifically as a quality check: every lemon on the shelves was a reason for a customer not to return. Weak covers were missed opportunities; to this day, Daunt remains one of the few people in the industry who can get the jacket of a major book redesigned.
Daunt Books grew for years as a quiet shop with a devoted following. “You felt the people who worked there were believers,” the actor Bill Nighy, a regular since the nineties, said. (He continues to give people its book-subscription service at Christmas. “If anyone knew how much time and money I spend in bookshops, they would say, ‘What the
fuck
?’ ” he said. “It is made more delicious by the fact that books were dead, officially, about ten years ago.”) In 1995, Daunt opened a second branch, in Belsize Park, and proceeded to expand to four more locations. He was dubious about publicity, so his booksellers, such as Diana Liu, learned to rustle up attention in other ways. In 2006, Liu, after being approached by Re-Wrap, a women’s textile coöperative in India, helped design the famous tote, which has an outline of the Marylebone shop façade. Alice Daunt, now a travel agent, told me that she had no idea her brother’s shop was a success until she spotted a Daunt Books bag hanging from a housekeeping cart “at some dreadful hotel in Antigua,” filled with soaps.
Buying a book demands an unusual commitment from the customer—hours, days, or even weeks of attention, and a measure of heart besides. Because the investment is great, the sales numbers can seem small. To reach the
Billboard
Top Ten, a music album often must sell about thirty thousand units a week; a book can make it to the
Times
best-seller list with a mere five thousand. An individual Barnes & Noble store might sell two dozen copies of a best-seller a week, and a “steady seller” might mean fewer than ten weekly sales.
Daunt Books’ figures, in this light, could be extraordinary. When the shop gave a paperback the treatment—a window, a display, and bookseller effort—it could expect to move a hundred and thirty copies a week. Once in a blue moon, a hardback attained those sales, too. The shop put on the map books such as Alexander McCall Smith’s “
The No. 1 Ladies’ Detective Agency
,” a previously obscure crime novel set in Botswana which became a best-selling series and a TV show. After Daunt came in one day buzzing about “
Two Jews on a Train
,” a collection of the French Hungarian writer Adam Biro’s folksy tales, his sellers got behind the book so enthusiastically that he asked the publisher, University of Chicago Press, for thousands more copies. The press refused, suspecting that the request was a hoax. Daunt suggested that Liu, who had moved to London from San Francisco, call them. “He said, ‘Will you talk to them in American?’ ” she told me. “I said, ‘I’m standing here, selling these books.’ And they asked, ‘
Why
?’ ”
“James was quite outspoken about the idea that many publishers didn’t really know what they were doing,” Macaulay, who is now the publishing director at Pushkin Press, told me. In 2010, he asked her to launch an imprint, Daunt Books Publishing, that would focus on out-of-print material and new manuscripts; she spent her first year in the publisher’s job filling in as a bookseller and found it instructive. “Standing behind the counter, you have thirty seconds or less to say the right formulation of words that will make the customer pick up
that book
and take it home,” she said. Even now, the shop floor must sign off on the imprint’s acquisitions and covers. “I have to think, What will a bookseller be excited to sell?,” Marigold Atkey, the current publisher, explained.
As a book buyer, Daunt had exceptional confidence. “James discovered that you could go to the publisher and say, ‘Will you give us better terms on this book?,’ ” Wolstencroft told me. During one standoff, as he recalled it, Daunt threatened to send the books back. (Daunt disputed the memory, denying that he would have done this.) “It seemed remarkable at the time, not just to me but to other people in the trade,” Wolstencroft said. “Other people prefer a collegial sort of management.”
Before the nineteen-nineties, bookselling wasn’t a business predicated on growth. There were chains (Brentano’s, Foyles), big chains (Borders), and really enormous stores (Powell’s, the Strand), but all of them expanded linearly. That changed in 1995, when Jeff Bezos launched his online bookstore, Amazon, on the theory, as the reporter Brad Stone put it in “
The Everything Store
,” that books “were pure commodities.” Though Bezos was technically a bookseller, his interest was in infrastructure. If you could sell people books efficiently, he thought, you could sell them laundry detergent, tube socks, and printers. Bezos spent a lot of effort, and magnitudes of capital, building a proud, sleek, global machine for frictionless selling. Its product was anything and everything—basically, stuff.
The idea that consumer companies are in the stuff business is still Amazon’s longest shadow. Enterprises plowing the creative fields now call their products “content.” People who might once have referred to books or photographs or rom-coms find themselves obliged, at least once a quarter, to speak of content as a kind of goo subjected to important active verbs. We generate content, publish it, surface it, and deliver it. Since “content” encompasses mystery novels, cheesecake recipes, “
Soul on Ice
,” breaking news, red-carpet commentary, videos of twerking cats, and the late writings of Heidegger, those verbs are the important thing. If goods are interchangeable—if it’s all just stuff—then market success must be the result of efficiencies in the delivery systems, and we are wise to focus on those, not the qualities of individual works.
By 2011, Daunt had developed a different philosophy. He had spent two decades on the shop floor, studying what customers bought and didn’t buy and why. Books, he knew, were not like laundry detergent. Decisions rarely happened categorically or in bulk; everything came down to whether the specific thing in front of you—
that book
, this shop—was good enough to draw you in. If powerful growth was to be had in the book business, that specificity would have to remain central. It was around this time that Daunt’s colleagues noticed a distance in him. “He’s ambitious,” Liu told me. “And I could suddenly feel that he wasn’t going to be held by Daunt Books.”
Only Wolstencroft knew that Daunt had by then spent two years trying to line up a purchaser for Waterstones, which operated some three hundred stores. The chain had been taken up into a conglomerate called the HMV Group, which, rattled by Amazon, had centralized warehouse operations and optimized pipelines. But those efforts failed to attract customers, and Daunt watched as Waterstones’ sales went into free fall, threatening to pull down much of the publishing industry with it. He took it upon himself to intervene. In early 2010, he got a call from Dennis Stevenson, a member of the House of Lords.
“I am literally having a cup of tea with a Russian businessman,” Stevenson said. “I’ve explained that there’s a bookseller who thinks that Waterstones can be saved. Why don’t you pedal over here and see whether you can interest him?”
The Russian, Alexander Mamut, was not an obvious savior. In the nineties, he had been known as “the Yeltsin family banker,” and emerged with fingers in the usual pies: fuel, telecoms, media. He was alleged to have been implicated in the Bank of New York money-laundering scandal—which transferred Russian capital through U.S. bank accounts—though nothing was proved. (Mamut denied any knowledge of the illegal money transfers.) He was also a prolific reader who, in 2004, had invested in the Moscow chain Bookberry. For two years, he had been quietly buying up shares of HMV, trying to precipitate a Waterstones deal. Daunt made a simple pitch about Waterstones’ shops: “If we save them, then we’ve got a perfectly nice little business, and we can turn a dime on it as well.”
Mamut asked how much it would cost. When Daunt said forty million pounds, the businessman looked pleased. “That’s less than Fernando Torres,” he later said. (His fellow-oligarch Roman Abramovich had signed Torres, a soccer player, for Chelsea F.C.) “It’s not even half a boat,” he added. Daunt recognized the signs of a man talking himself into a large purchase.
In the end, Mamut’s fund bought Waterstones for fifty-three million pounds. Daunt took Liu and Wolstencroft to a pub lunch and told them that he would be leaving Daunt Books to become Waterstones’ managing director. (He continues to own the Daunt shops.) “I was, like, ‘Oh, God, the banker within you is coming out,’ ” his sister Alice told me.
At Waterstones, Daunt spent three months interviewing employees—“Just, ‘What do you do?’ ” he said. He asked all four hundred employees in the home office to reapply for their jobs, and fired two hundred. “There’s nothing good—ever—about sacking,” he told me, sounding only slightly defensive. “The narrative is that everybody is a fantastic bookseller, loving books, but it isn’t the case. You have a disenchanted, unempowered, fairly miserable group of people, some of whom really are not good at their roles and are actively counterproductive. These people have to be moved on if you want to run a good shop. It’s a brutal process, and the store managers will never do it.”

In Daunt’s view, Waterstones’ trouble was that its previous owners had run it as a stuff company, where books were mixed with things like scented candles and decision-making was centralized. But he did notice exceptions. One day, he visited a Waterstones in Horsham, south of London, and caught the manager, Kurde Atfield, unawares. Her store was, as she puts it, eccentric. Her displays didn’t feature approved books, and they were decorated with handwritten signs and dusty plastic flowers. “A customer once said to me, ‘It’s like coming to my aunt’s house,’ ” she said. “I thought, James Daunt is going to go a bit mad.”
Daunt did go a bit mad in Atfield’s store (“Every time you walk in there, you just hold your head in your hands,” he has said), but he also thought she was a genius. The shop had become a community hub, with a strong sense of Horsham’s local interests and taste. He looked for other sellers at the company with similar instincts.
“James scythed through the head office—they didn’t understand what we were doing,” Luke Taylor, a quick-talking manager in his forties, told me in Waterstones’ six-floor Piccadilly store, above which Daunt had moved the company’s headquarters after closing remote offices. Waterstones had previously churned through young employees, so Daunt set up six major promotion points, with salary increases at each, allowing the most talented booksellers to grow across a full career. Taylor, an early beneficiary of these reforms, had been promoted to the position of retail director. “In 2012, there was an ice-cream freezer in the front and a wall of clearance DVDs right here,” he said, gazing out across the main floor, now filled with Dauntian round tables stacked with books.
By the numbers, the Waterstones turnaround was remarkable. Returns, the unsold books that shops send back to publishers, fell from twenty-five per cent of the stock to four per cent. The company’s forty-three-million-pound loss in 2011 became an eighteen-million-pound profit by 2017. Daunt eliminated “co-op”—the long-standing practice by which publishers would pay for placement in a bookstore. Instead, booksellers ran with their own ideas. To sell Gabrielle Zevin’s “
Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow
,” a novel of gaming, in 2022, Waterstones’ flagship set up an arcade machine loaded with Donkey Kong. For the release of “
Land
,” Maggie O’Farrell’s new potato-famine-and-cartography novel, it hired a fiddler to play in the window. This year, after hundreds of Waterstones booksellers voted to bestow the chain’s Debut Fiction Prize on “
May We Feed the King
,” a novel by the poet Rebecca Perry, the book landed on the British best-seller lists and was short-listed for the Booker Prize. To Daunt’s admirers, this is democratization. “In the pre-James world, when the books were chosen by a center, you couldn’t really have those surprise hits in the same way,” the chain’s head of books, Bea Carvalho, who also runs the prizes, said.
Yet publishers complained to me about a new consolidation of power. To keep returns low, Daunt shops often placed tiny initial orders, a wan show of confidence that risked seeping down to the fragile economy of the writing life. Jordan Pavlin, the Knopf publisher, described it as “challenging”: “We have to remain undeterred by those initials—we have to maintain our conviction and our vision for a book’s ultimate potential.”
As time went on, Waterstones seemed to put Daunt’s roles as a bookseller and a businessman into collision. In 2019, a platform called Organise approached employees to help them arrange a campaign to increase wages among entry-level booksellers to nine pounds an hour (slightly more in London), which fewer than half of Waterstones’ employees were earning. They circulated a petition, which received ninety-three hundred signatures. A second petition carried the signatures of twenty-four hundred writers, including novelists such as Sally Rooney. Daunt offered the employees a four-per-cent bonus but denied the base-wage increase. “The booksellers we were working with decided that they’d said what they wanted to,” Usman Mohammed, a founding member of Organise, said. “But they still weren’t happy with their pay.”
When I asked Daunt about his handling of the dispute, he told me that he saw nothing exceptional in it. “Pay is a zero-sum game,” he said. “If I’m going to pay one person more, I have to pay another person less. Are we putting that money into base pay, or into the career ladder?” (Mohammed called this “textbook corporate speech, where they draw a false binary.”) Daunt described himself as sympathetic, but told me, “The brutal economics of it is Sorry, our priority is the career.”
In 2014,
Russia invaded Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula
, and Western banks pulled back on lending to Russians. Waterstones, under Mamut, was unable to get the loans that British booksellers typically use to stock their shelves. “We needed a strong partner that would open the doors to the banks to us,” Marina Grönberg, who oversaw the day-to-day of Mamut’s businesses outside Russia, told me. In April, 2018, Mamut sold Waterstones to the private-equity arm of Elliott Management for a hundred and ninety million pounds, nearly a hundred and fifty million more than he had paid. In financial terms, the deal was an apparent victory, but Mamut took it as a bittersweet loss. “Alexander didn’t want to sell control—he hoped to remain with fifty-one per cent,” Grönberg told me. “Also, the reputation of Elliott is not necessarily of a friendly investor.” The firm had made its name as an activist hedge fund investing in distressed sovereign debt.
Mamut and Grönberg were persuaded by Paul Best, a new arrival at Elliott, who believed that the eclipse of brick-and-mortar retail by online commerce had been overstated, and that certain chains could flourish if well capitalized. Waterstones was his first acquisition. A source close to the deal said that Daunt was seen as key to the chain’s prospects. “In a lot of businesses, like fashion, you have the designer and then you have the C.E.O., a left brain and a right brain,” the person said. “He has both. If you put him in a room full of booksellers, they think he’s one of them, because he is. If you put him in a board meeting, he can talk about productivity, inventory turns, return rates.”
What followed was an astonishing period in which almost all British chain bookselling consolidated itself under one man. That September, Waterstones bought the troubled Foyles. In 2022, it bought Blackwell’s, too. Both of their owners, Christopher Foyle and Toby Blackwell, had contacted Daunt personally to offer him their failing enterprises; Daunt had come up with a rescue method. “Do nothing for a year,” he explained. “Let the shops get over the horror of being owned by a chain or whatever it is. Then say, How are you going to run this place properly? You didn’t go bankrupt because you were
such
a good bookstore.” Only then did Daunt put money in, to sparkle up the facilities.
Barnes & Noble, a publicly traded company that had begun its own stock-market slide, had been in Mamut’s sights before his exit. In 2019, Elliott contemplated an acquisition. “I think it’s doing the same things wrong that Waterstones was,” Daunt told Best. Elliott took Barnes & Noble private, for six hundred and eighty-three million dollars, inclusive of debt.
The American publishing industry watched the transaction with both relief and trepidation: it had heard the buzz of private-equity chainsaws on its grounds before. In 2006, in a notorious case, Pershing Square Capital Management, the hedge fund founded and managed by the billionaire Bill Ackman, had begun taking on a plurality stake in Borders, which operated about a thousand book-and-music stores. Pershing Square saw it as an undervalued asset. Yet, when Borders put itself up for sale during the credit squeeze of 2008, it got no offers. Pershing Square extended more debt. In 2010, Ackman made a failed bid to merge Borders with Barnes & Noble. That holiday season, Borders stopped paying some landlords and suppliers on time, and, in February, it filed for Chapter 11. Soon a thousand American bookstores had disappeared.
The prospect of Daunt’s leadership struck publishers as a flash of hope. “I’m generally not a booster,” one said. “But, you have to understand, we’ve had so much worse, just a legacy of morons and horrible people.”
Daunt told me, “Barnes & Noble
shouldn’t
be owned by private equity.” He saw it as a safe haven for a company that had needed to find its footing before proving itself. A few years ago, the podcaster Nigel Beale asked him whether Paul Singer, Elliott’s founder and president, was a lover of books. “No, he’s a lover of making money,” Daunt shot back, with what sounded like pride. At a moment when anything to do with reading or literature tended to be presented as a sympathy cause, like saving the whales, he’d got bookselling enshrined as that truly unassailable thing: a lucrative American business.
Yet public trust has not entirely followed him. Last spring, a mild fracas erupted when Daunt was quoted as saying that Barnes & Noble would stock and sell books written by A.I. “What I actually said was ‘We
don’t
sell A.I. books. We go to extreme lengths not to,’ ” he told me. “Then the next question is ‘Would you
ever
?’ ” He told me he said yes with a thought to word-game compilations and other non-narrative materials that publishers might churn out using A.I.
The tenor of alarm about new technologies was familiar. When Daunt arrived at Waterstones, bookselling was in a panic about the Kindle, said to be poised to replace paper books. Daunt was doubtful: he’d used the product. And he’d seen the advent of the personal computer during his time as a banker, when the arrival of the I.B.M. XT had carried him and his peers up the ranks. But books were more like rubber bands or bottle openers than like computers: their form was largely unimprovable for their function. Daunt had the Kindles displayed in every Waterstones. They sold quickly at first, then slowly, and then, booksellers told me, Kindle buyers began returning for books. Today, the e-reader market has plateaued at some ten per cent of traditional publishers’ revenue, while about seventy-five per cent comes from paper books, a technology essentially unchanged since the nineteenth century.
Now we are having a Kindle moment with A.I., which has seemingly started to affect the sales of self-help and pop-business titles—the kinds of books, Joel Miller pointed out to me, that present themselves as answers to such prompts as “How do I” or “I want to.” But the claim that A.I. writing threatens to replace novels, archival histories, reported narrative, and so on, seems a naïve insult to readers, and major publishers have avoided A.I. work. As far as the shelves of the bookstore are concerned, A.I. writing is a technology without a market.
The future of an industry is harder to judge. An enterprise consolidated under a single deft leader is secure until that leader leaves; then it’s just consolidated, and vulnerable. When I asked Daunt about succession, he insisted that he had stocked the upper ranks of both Waterstones and Barnes & Noble with like-minded booksellers who would carry on without him—unless, that is, a new owner did as he had done, and cleared the decks before charting a new course. Daunt told me he was sanguine. “If the whole thing is working well enough, they’ll let you get on with it,” he said.
Daunt spends most weekends when he’s in the U.K. at a house in Suffolk, a bike ride’s distance from the English shore. One morning, he met me at the end of the Darsham station’s platform with his car, an electric Polestar that was dark navy and caked in dust. “The filthiest car in Britain!” he announced and put the vehicle in gear.
East Suffolk, a windblown span of marshy coastland, has a reputation for stark, mournful beauty, and for drawing creative people with a taste for isolation and escape. This is the place that W. G. Sebald described, in “
The Rings of Saturn
,” as “dry, empty stretches of land which, by the end of a long summer, are almost like a desert.” Benjamin Britten’s opera “Peter Grimes” was set nearby. Daunt and Steward’s house is on what he describes as the emptier, inland side of the highway. Until the Waterstones job, which he accepted when his daughters were out of primary school, he would take off all their school vacations, and the family would travel together, often far afield. “We would go to Georgia, Nicaragua, Cuba, Ethiopia, and have a good, nice, proper, adventurous holiday,” he said. (“He’s what I call a
SFOG
, a smug father of girls,” said his sister Alice, who summarized his preferred style of travel less romantically: “At best, a really shitty tent.”)
Now Daunt gazed ahead as he followed the curves of road toward Southwold Books, a Waterstones shop that operates under its own name. Southwold is one of Britain’s affluent seaside getaway towns, filled with Range Rovers and sunburned Londoners. Daunt made a series of small groaning noises on the approach. “Obviously, I’ve gone into the grubby world of commerce,” he told me. “But whether you’re a civil servant, as my father was and my elder daughter is, or a schoolteacher, as my grandfather was, or someone who works with hospitals, like my wife”—a policy expert who sits on the boards of an N.H.S. mental-health trust and the U.N. Refugee Agency—“public service seems to be what we gravitate toward.”
Daunt likes to think of his own service as the preservation of a kind of literary and civil space. He has been a noisy critic of closing libraries in Britain. His acquisitions have invariably been of cherished bookshops about to shutter, and he has pulled Barnes & Noble out of real-estate deals—recently in Washington State—on discovering that they would threaten an independent shop nearby. In Southwold, he backed delicately into a parking space along the town’s central embankment. The waves below were an uncouth olive-brine brown.
“Let’s take up the full width of the sidewalk so everybody knows how in love we are!”
Cartoon by Ellie Black
“Did you bring your swimming trunks?” Daunt asked merrily, and led me in a zigzag through the parking lot of the Adnams brewery, then out to the bookshop, a chip-shop-size storefront with a blue exterior. Inside, I saw what looked like a very fine small store. Daunt saw an array of signs and symbols that he could read. He noted where abutting shelves were set at different heights, signalling divisions in the stock. He clocked, from several feet away, a paperback from McNally Editions and a few hardcovers from Slightly Foxed, a more obscure house.
“You can see it’s got lots of tiny publishers,” he said excitedly, half to himself. “Quite an eccentric stock as you start looking.” He approached the checkout counter, where a young bookseller in a gingham dress was ringing up customers. “I wanted to introduce myself,” he said, placing all five fingertips on his chest. “I’m James Daunt.”
“Oh, my goodness!” the bookseller, Nina Wilkins, said, perhaps not entirely joyfully. “Oh, my
goodness!
”
“Nice and busy in the morning, isn’t it?” Daunt said. “And the shop’s looking lovely.”
Wilkins said, recovering, “Shall I call my manager, Steph?”
As Daunt waited, he checked the pyramids. Early on at Daunt Books, he and Wolstencroft found that, if they placed unknown début-fiction titles on their own, people shied away, but, if they interposed known books of a similar flavor, customers bought both. Presenting the new in the context of the old allowed readers to orient themselves.
The manager, Steph Burridge, appeared, her blond hair half gathered into a top bun. “Congratulations,” Daunt, who congratulates everyone, said.
“We pick a book, and it just flies,” Burridge said.
“I always say that, in small shops, you can be talking to somebody and selling the book to three other people,” Daunt said. He paused. “Anything for me while I’m here?”
“I think the shop should have an awning,” Burridge said. “I mentioned it, and I just got completely—”
“Would you e-mail me?” Daunt said. “You don’t need to say, ‘Hi, James, the weather’s lovely, blah blah blah.’ Just write an e-mail that says—”
“Awning,” Burridge guessed.
“Awning,” Daunt said, with a smile.
For most of us, ideas about the state of literature are the result of a cohort experience. Reading is private—or has been since at least the sixth century, before which the Western habit was to read everything aloud. But conversing about reading is a social activity. If you were of a certain cohort in a certain time, you might remember everybody talking about “
Primary Colors
,” or “
Guns, Germs, and Steel
,” or “
White Teeth
.” To be ensconced within a reading cohort is bliss, and falling off the cart can be demoralizing. “Within the industry, we’re very used to there being a golden age and it being just over,” one publisher told me dryly. “The moment of decline usually depends on the age of the person telling the story.”
It is also true that cohorts used to be mostly local, made up of people you could meet for lunch. Now they are, like everything, atomized and diffuse. “Readers are connecting with each other in small communities scattered all over the internet,” Kris Austin, the C.E.O. of the self-publishing platform Draft2Digital, which serves more than three hundred thousand authors, told me recently. “The big gatekeepers are less major players than they used to be, and authors are finding readers directly—or readers find
them
, and tell each other on social media.” It is easy to be snide about the way that taste hierarchies flatten on social media, but any writer who genuinely connects with readers isn’t working in vain. “A romance author might be able to release a book a month, and, if they have a thousand people who will buy all of their books, they’re making a good living,” Austin said. Rarely, somebody breaks out and gets picked up by a publisher, as with the best-selling romance writer Colleen Hoover. But a lot of reading today happens in diverse pods below the publishing industry’s waves.
Cartoon by Roz Chast
These reading habits often reach booksellers through BookTok—an ecosystem of literary influencers across social media. Barnes & Noble shops sometimes include BookTok recommendations on dedicated tables, which have helped move books; TikTok has translated into fifty million book sales across Europe, according to Nielsen. Still, these displays are not universally adored. (“I think it’s lazy bookselling,” Victoria Harty, the chain’s New York retail manager, told me.) Most BookTokers are young, and appeal to readers in the eighteen-to-forty age range. “I think people much older than me maybe wouldn’t see that their tastes align with mine,” Jack Edwards, a twenty-seven-year-old BookToker with four million followers, said.
Edwards, who recently reviewed both Alexandra Romanoff’s romance “
Big Fan
” and John Berger’s “
Ways of Seeing
,” began posting as a student at Durham University, in the U.K. He told me that a great number of his followers were interested in writing in translation. (Half of all translated fiction is now bought by people between the ages of thirteen and thirty-four.) “I think the reason is that we’ve grown up in the digital landscape and are used to scrolling on our phones and seeing people from many different countries,” he said. “We don’t question reading a book from Nicaragua or Ethiopia or Sri Lanka.” They are also tired of their feeds. Recent years have brought a huge market for books with decorated edges and embossed covers, and major fantasy books now sell out in large luxury editions—an enthusiasm that the agent Juliet Mushens, who represents a lot of best-selling fantasy books, attributed in part to Daunt’s emphasis on visual display.
“People are ravenous for content that isn’t on their laptop or their phone,” Eden Yonas, another preëminent BookToker (twenty-five years old, half a million followers), told me. “I love that now, when I’m sitting on the train in New York, I can look up and, instead of seeing people on their phones, see them reading a book. Three, four years ago, I didn’t see that.” Every bookseller I spoke to reported increased book-buying among young customers.
It is puzzling, then, that the world is filled with professors reporting that students can barely muddle through the reading on their syllabi. That complaint was the focus of Tyler Jagt’s recent
Chronicle of Higher Education
essay
“My Students Can’t Read,” which provoked a flurry of responses. Dorian Thornley, the proprietor of Westsider Rare and Used Books, on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, gives a basic literary-knowledge quiz to the young college graduates applying to work there, and has been appalled at the results. “They don’t know who wrote ‘Moby-Dick,’ ” he said. “They don’t know who wrote ‘The Magic Mountain.’ ” It’s not that they aren’t reading. (Thornley’s own teen-age son, he told me with a sigh, reads almost exclusively “politicized Y.A., over and over again.”) It’s that their canon is illegible to older readers.
The new reading wars, in that sense, are largely about the primacy of taste. “The confusing thing for people in the business is that the books folks love and want to recommend are not the books that people wanted to catch fire,” Michael Cader, the founder of
Publishers Lunch
, a publishing-industry newsletter, said. Felicity Blunt, a prominent literary agent at Curtis Brown, told me, “We are discovering that people are reading things that we weren’t expecting—and we are behind certain curves.” One of the most-read genres in the United States right now is romantasy, or romance in fantasy worlds; at bookstores, readers across the country queue down the sidewalks for midnight releases of new titles. Earlier this month, “
Threshing Day
,” a short-story collection by the romantasy writer Rebecca Yarros, débuted at No. 1 on both the print and the combined print-and-e-book
Times
best-seller lists, having sold, according to
Publishers Weekly
, nearly nine hundred thousand copies of its special-edition release in its first week, superseding a new John Grisham novel for the first time in four decades—a moment of generational change in best-seller publishing.
Romantasy is not many people’s idea of great literature. But, then, neither is a lot of “literary fiction.” “How many of these books will actually command a place on our shelves in ten years?” Daunt said of this year’s best-sellers. “
Very
few. But, boy, do you know them when you find them.” He recalled his thrill on reading “
Tinkers
,” Paul Harding’s slender début novel centered on the memories of a clock repairman, which was published by a small press and, in 2010, won the Pulitzer Prize.
The truth is that the distance from romantasy to “Tinkers” can be small. Most readers don’t cut their teeth on Robert Caro or Proust; they begin with the Sweet Valley Twins or Agatha Christie, and the habit of reading propels them toward more remarkable work. “If you’re strictly a romance reader, I’ll be, like, ‘Have you ever read Jane Austen?’ ” Yonas said. In London, the writer Tom Willis has become known for organizing the Soho Reading Series, a slate of literary readings and parties that have drawn more than ten thousand attendees over the past few years, feeding what he describes as an enormous appetite for a real, welcoming literary culture among the young. “I’ll put on a reading with a writer like Rob Doyle”—the Irish novelist—“and, after it, people are queuing up with their eyes lit up like in the frigging olden days,” he said. He launched a literary talk show this fall—one more person trying to make even the screens a bookish place.
“Reading, right now, feels like resilience,” Edwards told me. “It feels revolutionary to choose friction in a world increasingly being designed to reduce it through ChatGPT.”
In garrulous moods, Daunt likes to impart advice for young travellers. Make an effort with the lexicon: a hundred words of any language will get you far. In remote terrain, speak whatever language you speak worst: you’ll use more gestures and expressions, which will make your message clearer. (Daunt speaks Turkish in rural Japan.) Travelling, like reading, is a reminder of the impossibility of communicating across territories—but also evidence that, somehow, we always do.
The politics of bookselling, as Daunt sees them, are pragmatic and pluralist. “I think booksellers, as a tribe, almost universally believe in principles of liberalism, which means that we’re politically of the left—not in a punching-with-Bernie way, though plenty will be, but in a commitment to diverse societies,” he said. Under his aegis, Barnes & Noble has joined with publishers to wage legal battles against content restrictions in Texas and Virginia, like those used to limit the distribution of L.G.B.T.Q.-themed books. But it has also supported its shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming, which mounted a display of
MAGA
books: the local taste. “We can’t believe in free speech and the importance of resisting censorship and then censor ourselves,” Daunt said.
Back on the road, in Suffolk, he told me that Barnes & Noble was the most engaging work of his career. “Waterstones was a bigger train set: more tunnels, more things to set up. And then, when you get to Barnes & Noble, it’s a
whacking
big thing,” he said. We were stuck behind a slow truck on a two-lane highway; I could sense him waiting to lay into the pedal for a burst of speed.
We reached the town of Lowestoft. Once a thriving fishing center, it was now a place without an industry. The Waterstones shop sat on a wide main street of drugstores and budget-clothing chains in whose windows everything appeared to be on sale. “This is the less affluent white U.K. you’re seeing,” he said. “The places that have been left behind, that become breeding grounds for Reform”—the British far-right party.
The store was neatly ordered, with a table of romances near the entrance and a bright-emerald carpet: a relic of an older style of décor. Daunt had said before we entered that, of all the shops he was responsible for, those like Lowestoft were the ones of which he was proudest. “There will always be some version of a Southwold Books,” he said. “But no one today is opening a bookshop in Lowestoft. If this one leaves the high street, it’s gone.” As we watched, the manager, Alison Mason, went from table to table, adjusting books, as if preparing a home for a visiting friend.
Before Daunt left, he made a slow round of the store, studying its displays and stopping at the children’s section, into which, Mason said, kids and teen-agers flocked daily after school. In the early days, at his own shop, he had been known for his laconic style of selling. “Booksellers can sometimes say too much about a book, but James would never say too much,” Wolstencroft told me. When showing visitors around, Daunt would seem to notice a book on a table and ask whether they had read it. When the answer was no, he’d pick it up and appear to examine it, as if it were the only thing in sight, a precious object borne across the world. Then he would hand it over. “Just read it,” he’d say. ♦

epub_17.text:
By
S. M. Reznik
Neil and Brenda met just days after Neil invented his time machine, which proved to be a handy access pass. They watched the Beatles play at the Cavern Club. They figured out which religion’s version of God was the right one. They prevented the Hindenburg disaster. They watched the Ashton Kutcher film “The Butterfly Effect,” and undid their undoing of the Hindenburg disaster.
Eventually, they fell into a peaceful routine. Brenda would ask, “What should we do tonight?,” knowing that Neil would reply, “Sal’s?” To which Brenda would add, “2004.” (Sal’s was much cheaper in 2004.)
“I want to take you somewhere,” Neil said one night, after an expensive 2078 visit to Sal’s.
“Where?” Brenda asked.
“I want you to meet me as a kid,” Neil said. “There’s something I think about a lot, and I feel like you’d understand me better if you saw it for yourself.”
Neil and Brenda climbed into the time machine, and he set it to 1995. A lot of people think that time travel is instantaneous, but it literally takes six hours to fly a plane across the country. Why would time travel be different? It takes three nanoseconds to go back to 1995, then six hours to travel from Boston, where Neil and Brenda lived, to Los Angeles, where Neil grew up.
“I wish we could’ve Ubered to your house,” Brenda joked as she got out of the thirty-minute cab ride from LAX, which cost eight dollars.
“Sh-h-h, don’t let them hear us,” Neil whispered, gesturing to little Neil, who stood in a circle with four taller boys. In the center was an injured bird. Boy No. 1 taunted little Neil, “What, are you too scared to put it out of its misery?” Boy No. 2 shouted, “I want to see bird guts!” Boy No. 3 blew a raspberry. And Boy No. 4 did not know how to bully.
Little Neil mustered his courage and brought a hammer down on the bird. The boys’ callousness quickly turned to disgust, their contempt steadily aimed at Neil.
“You see?” old Neil asked Brenda. “It’s funny, watching it now as a thirty-six-year-old man. That bird obviously wasn’t going to make it. It honestly looked kind of dead before I even hit it with the hammer. What a relief. I’ve felt guilty about that forever.”
“You should,” Brenda replied. “That was majorly fucked up.”
“Wh-what?” Neil stuttered.
Just then, little Neil approached the couple and, through his tears, mumbled, “Excuse me. I don’t mean to bother you, but you both look upset.”
“Murderer!” Brenda yelled.
It was an awkward cross-country flight and then time travel back to Boston, 2026. As soon as they got home, Brenda packed her things and left. Neil didn’t go on another date for ten years; he time-travelled to 2036, to speed up the wait.
In 2036, Neil
met Florence, who was born in 2009, if you’re keeping track. A few weeks in, Neil posed the question “Can I take you somewhere?” Soon enough, Neil and Florence stood in front of Neil’s childhood home, in 1995.
“What are those kids doing over there?” Florence asked.
“Don’t mind them!” Neil said. “Watch, she’s about to do it.” From behind a tree, Neil and Florence observed Brenda scolding little Neil. “She calls me a murderer and everything!” he said. “I haven’t stopped thinking about it for ten years. Now you can finally understand this part of me.”
“Wow. You’ve been thinking about another woman for ten years?” Florence asked. “By the way, what you did to that bird was seriously fucked up.”
After Florence left
him, Neil gave up on love for ten days. He paused time so that he could grieve properly.
Then Neil met Carrie. “Why’d you want to show me this?” she asked Neil, after he’d taken her back to the bird-killing scene, in 1995. “That second bitch was right. Hell, if you brought me back in time just to watch another woman leave you, you’d damn sure better feel like crap. Also, I’m sorry to bring this up on vacation—but I don’t think this is working.”
“You brought me
here to watch someone dump you for bringing her here to watch someone dump you for bringing her here to watch someone dump you?” Hannah, Neil’s next girlfriend, asked. By this point, Neil had learned from his mistakes. He’d tinkered with the time-travel machine so that the only way his fellow-traveller could make it back safely was in his warm embrace. Hannah chose to stay in 1995.
Neil planned one
final trip. Because of all the Boston-L.A. travel, he had lots of Delta SkyMiles, so he often got upgraded. He comfortably cruised back to L.A., 1995, the day before the whole bird incident. He took the ailing bird from the drawer that little Neil had been keeping it in, and hid it in a nearby forest.
When Neil got back to 2026, he had no memory of killing the bird. Brenda had left him for some other reason, probably because he built a time machine that he used only for dates. ♦

Fiction
Appeasement, Ohio
By
George Saunders
Photograph by James L. Amos / Getty
Yeow, the old Ohio place. My cousin Maribeth looks about the same. Her son Kip’s a man now: big boy, around two-fifty, thick pink arms like tattooed hams.
I meet Carl, Maribeth’s third, possibly fourth, husband: nice guy, sprig of hair on the front of his head like a Kewpie, but white hair, not blond.
Also Mick, a pal of Kip’s.
Read an interview with the author for the story behind the story.
“Eggs?” Carl says.
“No, thanks,” I say.
“I will,” Kip says.
“Scrambled,” Mick says.
“Unless you boys no longer believe in eggs,” Carl says. “Or chickens. Mick, still believe in chickens?”
“Yes, sir, still believe in chickens,” Mick says, maintaining discipline.
Podcast: The Writer’s Voice
Listen to George Saunders read “Appeasement, Ohio.”
“Upstairs, in the attic?” Carl says. “Kip? A box of Civil War coat buttons, from your great-great-whoever. Plus his bayonet.”
“Anyone can make a button,” Mick says.
“Anyone can put a bayonet in an attic,” Kip says.
“Look how I trained him up,” Mick says.
I’m trying to connect the beaming giant that is Kip with the shy little guy I used to carry up to bed.
Carl sets down a plate of toast.
“Food for the brain trust,” he says.
“You’re being sarcastic,” says Mick.
“Ma’s a believer,” says Kip.
“Well, you kids make a strong case,” Maribeth says.
“For example,” says Kip, spinning his Dell around.
Headline: “
Gettysburg Archaeology Proves No Battle
.” Author: “Ned.” Photo: metal detector leaning against a palm tree. Nailed to the tree, a laminated sign: “Locale: Gettysburg, PA.”
“Zero palm trees in Pennsylvania,” Carl says.
“That you know of,” Kip says.
“That anyone knows of,” Carl says.
“What’s your source?” Mick says in a faux-military voice.
“Having been there many times,” Carl says.
“Have you walked literally every square foot of the state?” Mick says.
“Shit’s sake,” Carl says.
“Language,” Maribeth says. “We don’t swear in this house.”
After my diagnosis, I e-mailed Maribeth, not asking for anything, just sharing. Within an hour she wrote back: “I’ll do screening, also Kip will.” A week later: “I’m not right, but Kip says no problem.” “It will be a true honor,” Kip wrote. “Remember how fun when you lived with us, just super happy memories of what was otherwise rough time for me as kid.”
Not painful supposedly.
Still:
micro-slice, eyeball, hypodermic, inject
.
Imagine the generosity of that.
Kip runs upstairs to get ready. Mick refills his plate, drifts outside. Maribeth and I sit at Grandma’s old table.
A few things hang in the air between us.
From her side:

Text comes in: “Sorry couldn’t help you load,” it says. “Glad you got goods. See u soon. Am over by swings. Let’s rock.”
“Goods?” I text.
“Oops Leo that not for you,” he texts.
“What goods?” I text.
“N mind,” he texts.
Then: “Fuck just accidentally texted Leo about guns.”
“Still me,” I text.
“Leo please forget all texts,” he texts.
“Guns?” I text.
“Zero guns ha jst joking,” he texts.
Guns? In my car? Mick’s coming to get Kip? So they can “rock”?
Aren’t I now, as of right now, an accomplice?
Or accessory? Or whatever?
Shit.
I call 911.
“Guns, oof,” the operator says. “That’s bad. Also sounds like they’re more or less stealing your car.”
“Only the one guy,” I say. “Mick. The other guy, the one hiding out in the park? Good kid. Unarmed.”
“Unless the other guy already got to him with the guns,” she says.
“Maybe get over there quick,” I say.
“Good idea, sir,” she says. “Normally, in cases where we’ve been looking for a guy and someone tells us where he is, and that there might now be guns involved, what we like to do is wait, like, three hours.”
“Sorry,” I say.
“You’re good,” she says. “Just saying. Long shift.”
Is it right? That I’ve called it in? Ratted Kip out? Maybe. Maybe, in a few years, here’s Kip, out of jail, doing dishes. His kids are in the yard, his wife’s on the couch. He’s thinking, Wow, can’t believe I used to think the Civil War was fake. But now look at me: a husband, a father. How’d I get here? Who helped me? By calling the cops on me that time I was hiding out in Witness Park and sending me to jail, which turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to me?
Leo did. Leo saved me.
With his love, his tough love.
In April, I had my third Boxton Event (BE), my worst one yet: three pyramidal blobs came zinging at me as I sat in the showroom reading the Buick paint guide. Around that same time, near my house, this guy who’d had Boxton’s for two years BE-ed badly as he and his wife drove across the Elbow River Bridge. Into the Elbow they went. The guy went right to shore, the wife drowned while paddling around looking for him.
That’s where I’m headed.
I ask the operator: Once they get Kip, might I bail him out? Bailed out, might he be allowed to come down to the clinic? Just for, say, three afternoons, for the one remaining left-eye graft, then the two right-eye grafts?
The cow-cat, sitting in the window, gives me a look, like,
Leo, really? Thinking about our eyes at a time like this?
The operator seems to feel the same way.
“Not following, sir,” she says. “That sounds like
you
stuff. This is
law
stuff. Let me get off, put this thing in motion.”
There are moments in life when suddenly there you are, the real you. Here I am. All those years, I had no use for these people. Then I did. Now I don’t. With Kip on his way to jail, I don’t.
I don’t actually, to tell the truth, think all that highly of them.
I love them but don’t think that highly of them.
This is going to be in the papers. And on the internet. And we get the paper at the dealership. And have the internet. Eugene reads the paper every morning. Sometimes while on the internet.
And I’ve just lost his loaner.
Time to clear out.
Maribeth’s got me in the downstairs bedroom that Grandma used to call Crap Central.
Grandma’s old sewing machine is in here, plus a treadmill, a wedding arch, years of tax returns in boxes, and, hanging down from the ceiling, a sheet of sheer red fabric from back when Maribeth ran her low-rent puppet theatre, Hands Within. On a shelf is a photo of Grandpa in his Army uniform, in Europe, just after he and his pals liberated some minor death camp he always claimed he couldn’t remember the name of.
I drag my duffel into the kitchen, take a last look around.
Goodbye, old house. Probably never see you again.
Maribeth and Carl burst in.
“He’s nowhere,” she says.
“Total madhouse at the battlefield,” Carl says. “Cops outnumbered by three to one. Then the mob went in and nabbed the books out of the gift shop. And knocked down the history plaques. After which three drunk gals loaded the old cannon up in their big-ass Silverado.”
“Oh, God, Carl, stop talking, make yourself useful,” she says. “Go take out the garbage or something. Jesus H. Christ. Let me think.”
“On it,” Carl says, and scoots off in search of some garbage.
I need to tell her.
That I just ratted out her kid.
Seeing her now, beside herself, cheeks hot, hair all over the place, I realize, not only do I love her, I do think highly of her.
I do.
Dear Maribeth.
So unlucky.
My phone rings.
“That him?” she says.
It’s Dr. Dalwani, from the clinic.
I step into Crap Central, take the call.
“So, your first set of slides are in,” Dalwani says. “Very happy results. Your left eye is now like the proverbial wise bridesmaid: attentive, amenable, ready to receive. Tomorrow we’ll grab the second left-eye graft from that enormous cousin of yours. Quite a character, that one. Did you know, he told me he thinks the Civil War wasn’t real? Crazy stuff.”
Then seems to catch herself, in case I’m also a nonbeliever.
“I hope I haven’t offended,” she says.
“Not at all,” I say. “I know the Civil War was real.”
“Well, I agree with you on that one,” she says.
Then a little silence, as in: Let’s reflect a bit on how interesting it is to have to even say that.
“See you tomorrow,” she says.
Don’t have the heart to say, “Actually, you won’t. My donor is, right this minute, being arrested.”
“Let’s do this! Let’s avert some blindness,” she says.
Kip knew, he knew how much I needed this. And still went out to that battlefield and did his silly shit.
Idiot.
Selfish idiot.
This is on him.
Carl leans in, a triangle of packing peanuts on his shirt, one arm behind his back.
“Dumpster was full,” he says. “To get our crap in, I had to move some junk around. And
voilà
.”
From out behind his back comes Kip’s portfolio.
I try to look like I haven’t seen it before.
“Especially please note this,” he says.
Tucked in a slit in the back cover is a Cabello’s receipt for six rifles, ten smoke grenades, two hunting knives, a hundred zip ties, three KitKats. Stapled to the receipt: a Polaroid of the rifles, grenades, knives, and zip ties piled up on a table in what looks like a storage unit. Kip’s leaning into the frame, giving a thumbs-up, one of the KitKats in his mouth like a cigarillo.
“Bad, yes?” Carl says.
I show him Kip’s texts.
“Lord God,” he says. “They’re on the move.”
“I called it in,” I say.
“Good to know I’m not the only non-nutjob in this household,” he says.
“You two get lost?” Maribeth yells.
“Right there,” Carl yells.
“Because look who the cat dragged in,” she says.
Which is funny, because the cat-cow’s here in Crap Central with us, licking something off Carl’s boot.
Mick and Kip are out there eating from the same huge bag of chips.
Carl doesn’t miss a beat, just charges right over.
“Guns, geniuses?” he says. “I don’t believe it.”
“False, defamatory,” says Mick.
“Guns?” Maribeth says. “We don’t do guns in this house.”
“Says the lady who once put drugs in my lunch,” Kip says.
“Hash is not guns,” she says.
“Well, obviously, but,” Kip says.
“Read it and weep,” Carl says, slapping the Polaroid down on the table.
“It’s six frigging guns, Ma,” Kip says. “We need to be able to defend ourselves. People are nuts, people hate what we stand for.”
Cartoon by Mick Stevens
“I get that,” Maribeth says. “But you could’ve asked me first. That would’ve been polite, that would’ve been good manners.”
“Time’s short,” Mick says. “Notebook.”
“Don’t boss her,” says Carl.
Maribeth gets a notebook out of the junk drawer.
“No, a real one,” Mick says. “With a lock on it.”
“Like a diary,” says Maribeth.
“Not like a diary,” Mick says. “The exact opposite of a diary.”
Then a little silence, as we try to figure out what the exact opposite of a diary is.
“Oh, never mind,” says Mick. “Your one’s fine.”
Mick sits, curls his arm around the notebook, scrawls something down.
“I, Leo,” he reads aloud, “hereby gift my car to Kip and Mick, attesting that they did not steal or take it without my consent written permission.”
“A document like that could have what possible earthly legal validity?” Carl says.
“Jesus, speak English, Carl,” says Kip.
“I’m not signing that,” I say.
“Add whatever your last name is,” Mick says.
“Not happening,” I say.
“Might be,” he says.
And pulls a gun out from his jacket.
Small gun. Like a derringer.
Still.
Puts it to my head.
“Whoa, whoa, whoa,” says Maribeth. “Absolutely not.”
“In the old days,” Mick says, “men were routinely executed for the crime of treasonous betrayal.”
“Had to be you, Leo,” Kip says. “Nobody else knew where I was. If Mick hadn’t come cruising into that playground, lights off? I’d be fried right now. Because of you.”
Tough love, I try to say.
But my mouth’s gone dry, very dry.
“That closeness?” Kip says. “Back in the day? Was real. But now? You don’t know me. Do you think you know me?”
“No,” I say.
Something in the way I squeak it out seems to get to him, and, for a second, there it is, flickering across his face, the old sweetness. He’s sad to see me like this, pressed against the fridge, gun to my head. He’d like to say something to stop Mick from killing me.
But for some reason can’t.
Or won’t.
Anyway, doesn’t.
Just gives me a wink.
He never could wink right. Only with both eyes at once.
“Leo, sign, I beg you,” Carl says. “It’s not worth it.”
He’s right. It’s stupid, means nothing.
And I want to live.
I sign.
“Pretty shaky hand there, hoss,” Mick says.
Then points the gun at the ceiling, pulls the trigger.
It just makes that click.
“We always both knew it wasn’t loaded,” Kip says. “That’s why I was winking!”
“And you find that funny?” Maribeth says.
“Behold the downfall of a childhood hero,” Mick says. “The revolution topples another false idol.”
Carl stumbles over, tries to pry the gun away from Mick. I have no idea why. We all know it’s not loaded. They wind up in this tepid wrestle-off which indicates that neither has ever come close to fighting anyone before.
“Carl, I love you, but stand the fuck down,” Kip says, and grabs Carl by the shirt collar. Carl slips, falls. His head hits the table, a pitcher drops to the floor and explodes.
“If this is love,” he mumbles.
He’s on the floor, head in his hands.
“Sorry, man, did not mean for that to occur,” Kip says.
Carl’s phone is on the pass-through. Maribeth’s is on Grandma’s old table, where the same three coffee rings from the sixties still make the same old accidental partial Olympic symbol.
Mick sweeps both phones up.
“Leo?” he says. “More heroics?”
I hand mine over.
“Now you’re getting it,” Mick says. “We’re going to be taken seriously around here. And everywhere.”
“That gal is so hot,” Kip says.
Up on the little kitchen TV is Eden Rodenhigh, of “Past/Not Past.”
Eugene sometimes puts her on in the showroom after we close, just to make fun of her.
“Looks like a vampire,” says Kip.
“In a porn,” says Mick.
“Exactly,” says Kip.
Breaking news tonight, Rodenhigh says: In a secret vault in Baltimore, a stash of notarized documents has been found, signed by Civil War veterans, who, at the end of their lives, fessed up to the big scam. Also a list of the true names and addresses of all former slaves, along with their actual occupations and 1858 yearly incomes, which, surprising no one, were right on par with the incomes of similar whites.
“That’s it, there it is,” Kip says. “She just up and says it. What everybody’s thinking.”
“See, Carl?” says Mick. “Interesting ideas. Reasonable lady. Not some stupid bigot.”
“Wait, that’s me,” Kip says.
“Well, I’ll be damned,” Maribeth says.
Up on the TV, footage of Kip tossing the docent; a shirtless guy tearing off the cover of a book about Fort Sumter; three drunk ladies giving the finger to the historical cannon; Kip tossing the docent again, this time in slow motion.
“Tonight, in the heartland,” Rodenhigh’s saying, “homegrown patriots demonstrated a love for country seldom seen in parts of the nation dominated by the Brainwash Cohort.”
“Dude, you’re anointed,” says Mick.
“I cannot believe Eden frigging Rodenhigh knows who I am,” Kip says.
“And many more will soon know it,” Mick says.
“You have to admit,” Maribeth says, and trails off.
Kip goes over, takes her by the shoulders, and they do this weird, affectionate head bump that it seems they must do pretty often, given how naturally she lowers her head to receive it.
“Be proud, Ma,” he says. “Of me coming awake. And having a view not many can have.”
The drunkest of the three drunk ladies gives the historical cannon a kick, then does some comical hopping around, indicating, Ouch, my foot.
Then: an American flag in a wadded-up heap; the Visitor Center door lying splintered in the grass; a guy setting a pile of books aflame with a psychedelic-themed lighter.
“Ah, perfect, a book burning,” says Carl.
“Not a book burning, Carl,” says Mick.
“Fraudulent claim,” says Kip.
Mick goes over, raises his leg, drops his booted foot square on top of Carl’s head.
I can see from the look on Carl’s face that he’s thinking something like, If books are being burned, isn’t that, de facto, a book burning?
But he just closes his eyes, sits there quietly.
I close mine, too.
Dark, dark, dark. Good practice for what’s coming. At least nothing’s zinging suddenly out at me from various fields of utter darkness. Not yet.
“Let’s hit it,” Kip says.
The screen door cries
BACKyard
more peevishly than usual.
Maribeth drops into a chair, misses it, hits the floor.
“Oh, God, my baby,” she says.
Carl crawls to her, wraps his arms and legs around her.
“I’m here,” he says. “Right here with you, doll.”
“Air,” she says.
He unwraps his legs, leaves the arms. She squirms free. He drops a foot in her lap.
“Oh, Leo, your eyes,” she says. “I’m so sorry. If I could do it for you, I would. You know I would.”
And I do know it. If she could do it, she’d do it in a heartbeat. Because, once she decides she loves you, she never stops loving you, no matter what.
We need to call the cops now.
But don’t have a phone among us. ♦
By Deborah Treisman

The Art World
The Secret History of Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock
At the Met, a landmark exhibition doesn’t just show that the painters were equals. It makes it impossible to imagine their art existing without their marriage.
By
Zachary Fine
Pollock and Krasner in Springs, New York, in 1949. The couple lived and worked in a small farmhouse nearby.Photograph by Martha Holmes / LIFE Picture Collection / Shutterstock
New York City, 1936. A party around Christmas at the Artists Union on Ninth Street. One imagines a sugar-dusting of snow on the ground outside and “Santa Claus Is Comin’ to Town” on the radio. A man, drunk, swaggers over to a couple on the dance floor and inserts himself between them. He takes the woman in his arms, presumably to start dancing, but instead rubs his body onto hers and says, “Do you like to fuck?” She slaps him in the face.
And so begins the story of Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock. Well, sort of—Pollock sobered up and attempted to charm Krasner, and at the end of the night they went home together. An encounter like that would be memorable for most people, but somehow the pair forgot about each other for five years. Then, in 1941, the painter and writer John Graham invited Krasner to exhibit a piece in a show with works by Picasso, Braque, and Derain, along with a few American artists, including one called Pollock. The name didn’t ring a bell, but after Krasner learned that he lived around the corner from her, on Eighth Street, she paid him a visit:
When I knocked, he opened. I introduced myself and said we were both showing in the same show. I walked right in. What did I think? I was overwhelmed, bowled over that’s all. I saw all those marvelous paintings, I felt as if the floor was sinking . . . He was not a big man, but he gave the impression of being big. About five feet eleven. . . . His hands were fantastic, powerful hands. I wish there were photographs of his hands.
Krasner fell in love with Pollock on the spot. He took a bit more time to warm to her, but once he did she made everything possible. She introduced him to key artists and critics, such as Willem de Kooning and Clement Greenberg, nudging Pollock’s work forward and helping to secure his fame. She lobbied fiercely for him to gallerists and patrons, including Sidney Janis and Peggy Guggenheim. When Janis first came to see Pollock’s art, Pollock sat quietly in the corner, and Krasner explained what made the paintings valuable. May Rosenberg, the wife of the critic Harold Rosenberg, once visited Krasner’s studio and assumed that the man hanging around in dungarees, not saying much of anything, was an intellectually disabled janitor. For years, Pollock’s brother Sande had nursed him through alcoholism and breakdowns, but then Krasner stepped in. She bought his groceries, washed his clothes, cooked his food, and handled administrative tasks and emotional crises. She also sacrificed her painting. Krasner was the more trained and established artist, but, after she met Pollock, she barely finished a piece for three years.
The blockbuster that just opened at the Met, “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” is probably, canvas for canvas, the best painting show in America this year. It does something I thought impossible, which is make Abstract Expressionism—the most fossilized of American art movements—seem new again. The curators, David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, don’t accomplish this with appeals to timeliness or relevance but with a mighty selection of pieces—more than a hundred and twenty, from eighty-two different institutions—and smart exhibition design. The show is circular, starting and ending with Krasner, and roughly chronological, with a few exceptions. It begins in the nineteen-fifties, with some Krasner paintings that incorporate strips of Pollock’s own—a collaging of their life and work, the show’s main theme—then goes back to their apprentice days, in the thirties, when Krasner received her first dose of European modernism through Hans Hofmann, and Pollock, after wriggling from the grip of Thomas Hart Benton, the American regionalist painter, worked through Mexican muralism, American Indigenous art, and Picasso to find a style better suited to his psychosexual torments. In 1942, Krasner and Pollock shack up on Eighth Street, and the show takes off.
Pollock’s first batch of distinctive work appeared shortly after, with “Stenographic Figure” (1942), “The Moon Woman” (1942), and “Male and Female” (1942-43). Standing in a room with them, you’ll see the tension building between figuration and abstraction, between a descriptive line and a self-governed one. In “Stenographic Figure,” a painting that Peggy Guggenheim described as “dreadful” and that Mondrian called “the most interesting work I’ve seen so far in America,” Pollock paints a lively dinner-table exchange between two creatures with swirly arms. Inspired by a Miró retrospective from earlier that year, and having learned about Matisse via Krasner, Pollock trials a variety of marks, from broad, clean planes of blue, orange, and black to jazzy calligraphy. “Male and Female” pushes the blended approach further, with little ketchup and mustard tantrums set off by a crisp chalkboard column of numbers—the style, like the equation, not adding up. The one piece in the room that suggests what’s to come is “Gothic” (1944), in which scythe-shaped lines swing through the composition. There’s a two-stage process at work here: a black line that flows through the painting expressively, followed by a regulation of that flow with blue, orange, and pink highlights. There are no math problems or mangled body parts or other intimations of reality. The whole piece is about the free and rigorous interplay of line.
In 1945, Krasner and Pollock married and moved to Springs, a town in East Hampton, where they purchased a run-down farmhouse on a small plot of land. With only a few hundred locals and one saloon in town, there wasn’t much distraction. Their new life came with a couple of eccentricities, like a blowtorch they used to melt frozen toilet water in the winter and a pet crow named Caw-Caw, but the setting led to the most fruitful period of their relationship. In 1946, Krasner began working on a series of small, densely loaded canvases called “Little Images.” After years of angular still-lifes and nudes, she broke into all-over abstraction, caking her surfaces in color. Some of these canvases are built up with choppy brushwork, as in “Shattered Color” (1947); others are covered in what looks like a macerated and pastel pulp that has been attacked with the tines of a fork. The most surprising development, though, are the drizzles of paint. Right as Pollock was making his famous pivot, so, too, was Krasner.
From 1946 to 1947, Krasner and Pollock tilted their paintings from a vertical axis to a horizontal one: Pollock from easel to floor, performing his “drip” technique on unstretched canvas in a converted barn; Krasner, with pre-stretched canvas, working on a table in an upstairs bedroom of the house. All of the grandeur and energy of Pollock’s looping brambles and cords are clenched in Krasner’s versions. In two pieces from 1947 and 1948, she primes the canvas with smudges of blue, green, and orange, then rains down a comprehensive drizzle of black and white, choking all the color. The one that caught me off guard was “Abstract No. 2” (1946-48). Its white drips have the fluency and thickness of Pollock’s line, but they’re delivered with a strange twist: a web of black paint that obscures the rest of the canvas. It’s almost like you’re squinting at a Pollock with your eyelashes gating your vision. Was there something about the drips that Krasner didn’t want to see, or wanted to push away?
What happened next is now ancient chronicle: Pollock showed his new work at the Betty Parsons gallery in 1948;
Life
asked if he was the greatest painter in America; and the center of cultural gravity swung from Europe to the United States, from the Old World to the New. The provocation of Pollock’s work was so accessible, so instantly recognizable, that it’s easy to forget why the drip paintings weren’t just controversial but a referendum on the state of art, the nation, and the modern soul. Interpretations ran the gamut.
Were the paintings acts of negation—attempts to destroy figuration, to bring the history of painting to its knees—or triumphs of creation and renewal? Were they anti-capitalist traces of raw selfhood, or C.I.A.-boosted symbols of American freedom? Were they life-affirming “actions”—performances for which the paintings were just an interesting residue—or intricate exercises in self-conscious form? If your frame of reference was the Second World War, they might be images of the body blasted apart by shell fire. If your frame was psychoanalysis, they were glimpses of that dark, wordless corner of the mind called “the unconscious.” Some people experienced them as a purely optical means of aesthetic transport; others found in them tactile accumulations of crust, carnage, and debris. What made them so exciting, either way, was the immediacy they implied. The frozen velocity of paint whipped across a canvas suggested a new visual metaphor for intensity, aggression, violence, virility, force, energy, music, and ecstasy, a more efficient representation than any previous word or picture had managed.
Because we’ve cycled through all the responses to Abstract Expressionism, it would be easy to glide through the Met show in a reverential but dispassionate mood, feeling that every emotion is an ersatz emotion, every thought a rehashed one. But there’s a welcome lightness to the work in 2026, something you can find instantly in the show’s most spectacular room. Loosely modelled off “The Ideal Museum,” an unrealized gallery plan that Pollock developed with an architect and a friend, it features his colossal drip pieces—including “Lavender Mist,” “Autumn Rhythm,” and “One: Number 31, 1950”—and eight large canvases by Krasner. Each painting hangs on a freestanding wall, so you can pinball your way around them, discovering and rediscovering things. Standing just two feet away from “One,” I felt the wonderful disorientation that comes from looking at a Pollock: the disruption of a horizontal image by the memory of its vertical process. The frenzy of black, white, and turquoise fills your gaze with a completely weightless and floating image, just as you notice how every rope and droplet of paint has been pulled down by gravity into the fabric. Your mind’s eye is standing on the wall, but you’re still here, on the ground.
The other side of the room has eight of Krasner’s collage paintings, all produced in a sprint in 1955. Each is almost seven by five feet, and most establish a broad field of color—blue, crimson, orange—across which migrate sharp and irregular shapes, some like long teeth or spears, others like shards of obsidian. Together, they amount to a daring raid on the standard-bearers of Abstract Expressionism. By the late forties, many of the Ab Ex artists had regulated the expressive element of their style into signature trademarks—think of Rothko’s soft bars of color, Robert Motherwell’s enlarged ink stains, Adolph Gottlieb’s celestial orbs, Clyfford Still’s crags. In a savvy deflationary move, Krasner sliced and diced the machismo of Ab Ex into her own configurations. The vertical stripes in her paintings recall Barnett Newman’s “zips,” the black occupying shapes have a touch of Motherwell, and some edges are jagged enough to be by Still. The most provocative move is in “Bald Eagle” (1955), with fragments cut right out of a Pollock drip painting and packed into a mosaic—Krasner reclaiming her husband’s free-form mark with a blade. The critic Arthur Danto once wrote that, in Krasner’s work, “there are only shadows of other selves, the echo of other voices,” implying that she was doomed to be derivative. That not only ignores the cross-pollinating exchange with Pollock but also fails to see how her absorption of other modes, and her studied replication of expressive signatures, anticipates what was shortly to be celebrated as “postmodern” in the work of Jasper Johns and Robert Rauschenberg.
“Oh—I stopped listening after you said ‘needless to say.’ ”
Cartoon by Suzy Becker
Even as fame and alcoholism sunk Pollock in the fifties—his production tapered, and his affairs all but destroyed the marriage—he and Krasner started painting more like each other, not less. Compare Krasner’s “Untitled” (1951) to Pollock’s “Easter and the Totem” (1953), in which Krasner’s distinctive palette of Pepto-Bismol pink, pale orange, chalk white, and black gets reprised by Pollock, who also borrows some of his partner’s curvy Matisse-like forms. After Pollock spent years trying to keep the figure out of his pieces, recognizable lumps and body parts reëmerged, such as the whirlpool of drowning eyes in “Ocean Greyness” (1953), and the same ocular shapes rolled into Krasner’s work a few years later, in “Embrace” (1956). They both had a symbolic fetish for eyeballs, and it’s hard to tell if it was pantheistic or paranoid—every particle of nature seeing itself or watching them.
Greenberg said Pollock began to wobble at the end, and you can see why. There’s a tackiness to some of his final gestures, like “The Deep” (1953) and “Portrait and a Dream” (1953). “The Deep” I instinctively like: it has an almost baptismal quality, as though you’re lifting your head out of a bath of milk to see the night sky. But there’s also a melodrama to the way Pollock uses white paint to surround a black chasm that runs through the picture’s center, as if it were a wound or an existential abyss. Three years after making it, while driving drunk in East Hampton, Pollock crashed his car, killing himself and one of the passengers, Edith Metzger. (The other, Ruth Kligman, with whom he was having an affair, survived.) Krasner was in Paris, and Greenberg called her to deliver the news.
Krasner’s “Bald Eagle” (1955).Art work by Lee Krasner / Courtesy © 2026 Pollock-Krasner Foundation / ARS
But Krasner’s life kept going, and so does the exhibition. After Pollock died, she moved her studio into the barn at Springs and started painting on a grand scale, with pieces like “The Seasons” (1957), which is almost seventeen feet wide and eight feet tall. Filled with magnified pink and green foliate shapes, it’s like pressing your face into a basket of flowers or ripe fruit; the painting doesn’t turn inward to mourn but rather outward to nature. “I remember sitting with Jackson on our country porch,” Krasner said, “sitting there for hours, looking into the landscape, and always at dusk, when the woods ahead turned into strange, mystifying shapes.”
Unlike Pollock, who tended to settle into a style, Krasner stayed restless. In the sixties, she painted brown and stormy abstractions, where paint seems spit out of a fountain pen, as well as works of unbounded color and fluorescence, such as “Combat” (1965); in the seventies, she started cutting up a cache of her own charcoal drawings, and gluing them into fractured Cubo-Futurist collages. Until her death, in 1984, she was always casting back and lunging forward, tracing and retracing her steps. At the Met, one gets the impression that Pollock was a fascinating passenger whom Krasner picked up, travelled with for fifteen years, and kept talking to even once he was gone. After all, they were painters in love. They poured themselves into each other, and the show makes it impossible to think of them apart. ♦
